docs.t: Judge Robert N. Chatigny (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Robert N. Chatigny, D. Conn.. Trial: Trials run Monday through Thursday, 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Attach motions in limine to the joint trial memorandum, and they are decided at the final pretrial conference. Exhibits approved at that conference are pre-marked and in evidence. He asks the submitted voir dire questions and lets counsel follow up. Civil juries are eight with no alternates, juror notes are allowed, and the charge is given in writing. He grants a request for a concise, non-argumentative opening and usually gives one hour for closing with 15 minutes of rebuttal. No arguments in front of the jury, and raise procedural issues before or after the trial day or at breaks.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Discovery disputes: He tries to resolve discovery disputes by brief letters or a conference call and doesn’t allow discovery motions or briefs before the call. Follow his Instructions on Discovery Disputes. He decides most discovery disputes himself, and counsel must take part in conference calls, often on short notice. Don’t call chambers ex parte except to ask for a settlement conference, and have all parties on the line.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Motions: No sur-replies and no letter briefs: file a formal motion, and for new authority file a notice of supplemental authority. He has no individual rules on dispositive motions apart from valuing brevity, and pre-filing conferences aren’t required unless he orders one. For an urgent motion, file it and send chambers a copy with a short cover letter. No response to a motion for reconsideration unless he allows it, usually with the full 21 days from his order. Motions to extend time follow Local Rule 7(b).

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies: The next business day after e-filing, deliver one bound paper copy to the clerk’s office, printed from the docket with the ECF header, of TRO, preliminary injunction, and prejudgment remedy papers, summary judgment papers, joint trial memoranda, and trial briefs. Exhibits are separately tabbed. Cite exhibits by their CM/ECF names, and give each a cover sheet.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Argument and scheduling
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Argument and scheduling: He has no motion day and hears argument as his schedule allows, often ruling from the bench even on dispositive motions. He invites junior lawyers to argue and allows a second senior lawyer to argue for the same party. The Rule 26(f) report usually becomes the scheduling order, and he decides whether a scheduling conference is needed. A party seeking a stay of discovery must move for it. Motions for preliminary injunctions get an early telephone conference.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Settlement
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Settlement: He usually refers parties to mediation with a magistrate judge and invites a short joint request. The court won’t retain jurisdiction to enforce a confidential settlement unless the terms are put on the public record with reasons.

docs.t: Judge Michael P. Shea (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Michael P. Shea, D. Conn.. Trial: Typical trial days run 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., five days a week. Openings are very short and non-argumentative, and closings are generally 30 minutes. Exhibits are pre-marked and exchanged at least seven days before the joint trial memorandum, and unlisted exhibits aren’t admitted absent good cause. Motions in limine are due 30 days before the first pretrial conference. Civil juries are at least eight and usually nine, with note-taking, and he charges the jury before closings. No re-cross, and sidebars are rare.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Argument and rulings
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Argument and rulings: He doesn’t routinely hear argument but will ask for it if it would clarify an issue, and he considers requests after reading the papers. He may tell counsel beforehand which issues interest him. He rules from the bench on an ad hoc basis.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and conferences
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and conferences: He uses the report to spot inefficiencies and routinely schedules a telephone conference. He usually reads new complaints before the report comes in, to check for conflicts and issues that might need his attention. He may use pre-argument conferences on dispositive motions, for example to get an amended complaint instead of a ruling on a motion to dismiss, or to simplify a complaint when a motion to amend is filed.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Briefs and affidavits
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Briefs and affidavits: File a motion for permission, stating the basis, before a sur-reply. He discourages letter briefs. To raise new case law, file a request for leave to file a supplemental brief with the brief and the cases attached. He doesn’t favor lawyer affidavits, since he treats all statements by counsel as representations to the court. He reads reconsideration motions carefully for whether they meet the procedural requirements.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies and extensions
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies and extensions: He prefers chambers’ copies, and the requirements are in the electronic filing order entered on the docket in each case. He usually grants extensions unless good cause is missing or the privilege has been abused.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Discovery and settlement
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Discovery and settlement: He frequently but not always refers discovery motions to a magistrate judge and usually tries to resolve the rest by conference call. He prefers not to hold settlement conferences himself and refers them to a magistrate judge or a para-judicial officer.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Emergency relief
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Emergency relief: Before acting on a TRO motion he usually seeks the defendant’s input. He has no set procedure for preliminary injunctions but often asks if the parties will consolidate the hearing with the final hearing. He typically refers prejudgment-remedy motions to a magistrate judge.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Joint trial memorandum and motions in limine
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Joint trial memorandum and motions in limine: Dispose of all motions before you file the joint trial memorandum, and file any motions in limine with it. He wants Daubert and other motions in limine raised in advance, preferably by the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Alvin W. Thompson (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Alvin W. Thompson, D. Conn.. Trial: He generally starts between 9:30 and 10:00 a.m. and runs to 4:30 or 5:00, with two 15-minute breaks and a 45-minute to one-hour lunch, five days a week, and he starts on time. He doesn’t usually limit trial or witness time, but may split the time if estimates look excessive. He suggests ten minutes per side for openings and sets closings with counsel, from half an hour to an hour and a half. Objections during closing may be sustained. At the final pretrial conference he asks what demonstratives you have and whether you want court equipment to show them. He generally doesn’t admit them as full exhibits but allows marking for identification, and encourages exchanging them early. Stipulate to as many exhibits as possible. Pre-mark all exhibits and submit them to him in binders at least three days before trial. The pre-marked numbers are the trial nu

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and schedule
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and schedule: He treats the Rule 26(f) report as critical, and his courtroom deputy sends a notice if it is late. Every proposed date must fall on a Friday. The report must show you consulted your clients (and known witnesses if needed), give a meaningful overview including whether claims can be narrowed and whether settlement talks would help now, and use realistic dates built for the case. Beyond Form 26(f), add a Subsection V.E.1 with a date for a post-discovery telephone status conference, no earlier than two weeks after discovery closes and before the dispositive-motion deadline. If dispositive motions are filed, the joint trial memorandum is due within 30 days of the ruling and the case is trial-ready 30 days after that. If none are filed, the memorandum is due 45 days after discovery closes and trial-ready 45 days after the memor

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Motions and argument
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Motions and argument: He hears argument on dispositive motions to address questions counsel can resolve in person, and on non-dispositive motions only when it will materially advance the case. He may rule from the bench. Sur-replies are rarely needed: file a motion for permission with the brief. Don’t file letter briefs unless he asks; file a formal motion instead, and use a notice of supplemental authority for new cases. For urgent motions, file with the Clerk and send chambers a copy with a short cover letter explaining the urgency. Attorney affidavits aren’t needed to identify exhibits or deposition transcripts on dispositive motions, and he rarely accepts them as evidence on disputed facts other than attorneys’ fees.

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Extensions
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Extensions: He is likely to grant an extension when all parties consent and it doesn’t affect the scheduling order. Otherwise Local Rule 7(b) good cause applies. He asks that, absent extraordinary or supervening circumstances, you file at least seven calendar days before the date at issue.

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Discovery disputes: Don’t file a discovery motion until you have discussed the dispute with him. File a joint motion for a discovery conference that describes the dispute, says you conferred in good faith, lists the issues, and gives dates and times you’re available for a telephone conference. At least a week before the conference, each side files a brief of no more than 5 pages. He decides most disputes himself and may refer others to a randomly assigned magistrate judge.

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Emergency relief and copies
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Emergency relief and copies: No ex parte TRO without extraordinary circumstances, and he usually asks the lawyer to try to reach the other side by phone. Preliminary-injunction motions get an early telephone conference to see if discovery is needed and to encourage combining the hearing with a trial on the merits. Chambers’ courtesy copies of e-filed documents are not required.

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Trial: Typical days run 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with an hour for lunch and two 15-minute breaks, five days a week. Long cases may run 9:00 to 5:00 four days a week. He usually sets no time limits, but his pretrial order requires you to separate witnesses and exhibits you “intend” to call or use from those you “may.” Exhibits are pre-marked and exchanged under that order, with one set for him and one for his clerk. Openings in civil cases must be non-argumentative and usually run ten minutes or less; closings are generally 30 minutes. Disclose demonstratives before use; they can’t be used in closing unless marked as an exhibit or shared with the others at least a day earlier. File motions in limine with or before the joint trial memorandum. State objections in a few words with no argument; he rarely allows sidebars. Submit proposed jury instructions with t

docs.t: Judge Victor A. Bolden (D. Conn.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Victor A. Bolden, D. Conn.. Criminal cases: He is paired with Magistrate Judge Garfinkel for initial presentments, where a scheduling order with a jury selection date issues. Pleas are before him; call the number on his page to schedule one. A continuance motion that touches the Speedy Trial Act gets a telephone status conference and must come with a signed waiver from each defendant. In cases with identifiable victims, the prosecutor must email the chambers law clerk at least 24 hours before any public proceeding to certify compliance with the Crime Victims’ Rights Act.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Argument and rulings
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Argument and rulings: He hears argument on dispositive motions when, after reading the papers, he still has questions counsel can resolve, and rarely grants one without letting counsel argue. He hears non-dispositive motions only when argument will materially advance the case. He often schedules dispositive motions for a motion day and rules from the bench, even on dispositive motions.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and conferences
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and conferences: If your deadlines are reasonable, the report becomes the initial scheduling order. It should give a meaningful overview and help the parties consider narrowing claims and settlement. He generally honors requests for status or settlement conferences. Conference calls can replace most chambers conferences, and he requires counsel to join calls, often on short notice, when a prompt call will help. He encourages you to contact chambers when discovery disputes arise.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Briefs
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Briefs: Sur-replies are rarely necessary, but he generally grants a motion for leave. He occasionally asks for letter briefs, which are docketed as pleadings. Otherwise briefs must follow the Local Rules. Reconsideration motions must follow Local Rule 7(c). Lawyer affidavits may be used to identify exhibits and transcripts on dispositive motions, but are rarely if ever accepted as evidence on disputed facts other than attorneys’ fees.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies and extensions
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies and extensions: He appreciates copies of dispositive and emergency motions and trial memoranda, including requests to charge. Don’t send other filings. Print from the docket with the ECF header, use a three-ring binder if a staple won’t hold, and tab each exhibit separately. Double-sided is fine. Reasonable extension requests are generally granted. Negotiate one all parties accept and say it is on consent. State the reason and the number of earlier extensions.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Discovery and referrals
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Discovery and referrals: He prefers to resolve discovery disputes by conference call and decides most himself, referring a few to a magistrate judge. He doesn’t refer all motions of any one type, and referrals depend on each judge’s involvement and time and can be sent back. Even after briefing, he expects the parties to keep trying to resolve it, and costs may be awarded under Rule 37(a)(5) when the court has to step in.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Emergency relief
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Emergency relief: He is extremely reluctant to grant ex parte TROs and requires strict compliance with Rule 65. TRO and preliminary-injunction hearings are normally set by order to show cause, and when possible after a conference with all counsel. Put the precise relief you want in a draft order, and support it with a memorandum and non-attorney affidavits.

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Settlement and joint trial memoranda
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Settlement and joint trial memoranda: His status report orders require the parties to certify they discussed settlement in good faith since the order. He schedules a settlement conference on request or when it looks useful, usually with a magistrate judge or the special masters program. He encourages a settlement conference before you spend on the joint trial memorandum. The pretrial order calling for it issues after the dispositive-motion deadline, and a joint motion can postpone it if serious settlement talks are underway. His order is similar to, but not the same as, the standing order on trial memoranda. Send chambers a courtesy copy, including proposed findings or requests to charge. When the memorandum is ordered, the case goes on a trial calendar, and at the calendar call counsel report on the availability of parties and witnesses and jury sele

docs.t: Judge Stefan R. Underhill (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Stefan R. Underhill, D. Conn.. Trial: Lawyers report at 9:00 a.m. and the jury sits from about 9:30 to 5:00, five days a week. He keeps lawyers after 5:00 for objections. He sets no time limits but presses you to lower unreasonable estimates. His pretrial order requires separating witnesses and exhibits you “intend” to call or use from those you “may,” telling the other side the order of witnesses in advance, and exchanging pre-marked exhibits, with one set for him and one for his clerk. He encourages affidavits or color-coded deposition transcripts in place of direct testimony in bench trials and urgent matters when counsel agree. He routinely sequesters non-party and non-expert witnesses, even without a motion. He has rarely denied a civil opening but dislikes argument in them, and may interrupt an improper opening or closing without an objection. He has denied government opening

docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — Communicating with chambers
docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Communicating with chambers: He wants case-related questions handled through the docket, not by phone or email to chambers. He doesn’t accept informal letters from litigants or anyone else and has the Clerk return them unread.

docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — Pre-filing conference for dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Pre-filing conference for dispositive motions: Except in bankruptcy appeals, Social Security appeals, habeas cases, and pro se cases, you must request a pre-filing conference before moving to dismiss, for judgment on the pleadings, or for summary judgment. File a detailed letter motion of no more than three pages stating the basis for the motion and a proposed briefing schedule. Every party served must file a letter response of no more than three pages within five business days. The movant may not reply without leave. Serving the letter within the Rule 12 or 56 deadline counts as timely service of the motion. Ask for a motion-to-dismiss conference as soon as possible after the summons and complaint are served. For summary judgment, the movant’s letter must include a preliminary Local Rule 56(a)1 Statement, and the opponent has ten business days to file a

docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and discovery
docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and discovery: The report should give a meaningful overview and usually becomes the scheduling order. He prefers discovery to close within twelve months of the report and may enter a twelve-month cutoff even if you ask for longer unless you explain why. List actual deadline dates, even if tied to earlier events. A motion to dismiss doesn’t stay discovery or extend its deadline absent extraordinary circumstances and a filed, approved motion to stay. Parties may agree to move interim discovery deadlines without his approval so long as the deadline to finish all discovery doesn’t move. He may decide discovery disputes himself or refer them to a magistrate judge, and expects you to keep trying to resolve them even after briefing.

docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — Extensions
docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Extensions: File strictly under Local Rule 7(b): three business days ahead, the other side’s position, the number of earlier extensions, and particularized good cause. In criminal cases, every extension or continuance motion must also state any pending state criminal cases against the defendant, the charges, the date of the next state proceeding and whether it is a sentencing, and whether a state proceeding has identified victims, or say there are none. For an expedited ruling on an extension motion, send chambers a courtesy copy with a cover letter explaining why.

docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies and formatting
docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies and formatting: In a case with counsel, promptly send one courtesy hard copy of any filing that, with its exhibits, attachments, and memoranda, runs over 25 pages. This doesn’t apply to self-represented litigants or criminal cases. Print from the docket with the ECF header, order and tab, and bind with a three-ring binder or left-side binding if it can’t be stapled. File text-searchable PDFs. You needn’t attach unreported cases unless Westlaw doesn’t have them. Attorney affidavits aren’t needed to authenticate exhibits on dispositive motions unless there’s a known dispute.

docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — Argument and rulings
docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Argument and rulings: Ask for argument under Local Rule 7(a). He gives strong weight to a request but may rule without argument on a dispositive motion. There is no motion day. He is usually an active questioner. He ordinarily rules in writing but may rule from the bench, and you can get a copy from the court reporter. He lets a second senior lawyer argue so a junior lawyer can too.

docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — Settlement, referrals, and rescheduling
docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Settlement, referrals, and rescheduling: Nearly all civil cases settle, and he usually refers the parties to a magistrate judge at some point. To ask for a referral, file a joint statement (it can be a single sentence) or one party’s good-faith statement that all counsel conferred and agree. He encourages limited early discovery, perhaps one deposition per side, before mediation. To reschedule any proceeding, including a phone conference, file a motion with three alternate dates when all counsel are available, and state the other side’s position if it isn’t joint.

docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — Emergency relief and pleas
docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Emergency relief and pleas: No ex parte TRO without extraordinary circumstances, and he usually asks the lawyer to try to reach the other side by phone. Preliminary-injunction motions get an early phone conference, and he encourages combining the hearing with a trial on the merits. Prejudgment-remedy motions are often referred to a magistrate judge. For a change of plea, counsel must confer on the offense level, criminal history category and score before finalizing the written plea agreement, and email the final agreement to the courtroom deputy at least three business days before the hearing, or risk a continuance.

docs.t: Judge Vernon D. Oliver (D. Conn.) — AI policy and broadcasting
docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. AI policy and broadcasting: He has a no-tolerance policy for briefing, AI-assisted or not, that hallucinates legal propositions or badly misstates the law, and says such filings will often draw sanctions absent a reasonable excuse. Rule 11 applies fully to pro se litigants. He doesn’t allow remote public access to in-person proceedings and won’t provide links or dial-in information.

docs.x: Judge Vernon D. Oliver, D. Conn.. Trial: Jury selection is typically the third Tuesday of each month, lasting a half day to a full day. A trial day runs 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with a 45-minute lunch and two 15-minute breaks, four or five days a week, and counsel report at 9:00 and may need to stay late for objections. Civil openings are short, closings generally up to an hour per side. His Joint Trial Memorandum instructions control exhibits, and require motions in limine and proposed jury instructions with the memorandum. Civil juries are at least seven, usually eight, and may keep binders of exhibits in evidence and take notes. Ask permission to approach a witness or hand up a document and name the exhibit, and stand at the podium. Redirect is brief and limited to new issues, and he allows no re-cross. docs.t: Judge Kari A. Dooley (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies
docs.x: Judge Kari A. Dooley, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies: Unless she orders otherwise, deliver one paper copy, with all exhibits and attachments, of dispositive motions and their oppositions, joint trial memoranda, and post-trial briefs. Bind and tab them (tabs are appreciated, not required). If a staple or medium binder clip won’t hold the copy, use a three-ring binder or bind it on the left side. Double-sided printing is fine. Print every copy from the docket so it bears the CM/ECF header. In criminal cases courtesy copies aren’t required.

docs.t: Judge Kari A. Dooley (D. Conn.) — Formatting and affidavits
docs.x: Judge Kari A. Dooley, D. Conn.. Formatting and affidavits: File text-searchable (OCR) PDFs under the Electronic Filing Policies and Procedures. You needn’t attach unreported cases to a memorandum unless Westlaw doesn’t have them. Attorney affidavits aren’t required to identify or authenticate exhibits and transcripts on dispositive motions unless there’s a known dispute about a document.

docs.t: Judge Kari A. Dooley (D. Conn.) — Argument
docs.x: Judge Kari A. Dooley, D. Conn.. Argument: Ask for argument under Local Rule 7(a). If you ask on a dispositive motion she will generally schedule it unless she thinks it won’t help. She has no motion day. She doesn’t usually schedule argument on non-dispositive motions but will consider a request. She lets a second, more senior lawyer argue if that gives a junior lawyer a part.

docs.t: Judge Kari A. Dooley (D. Conn.) — Referrals and rescheduling
docs.x: Judge Kari A. Dooley, D. Conn.. Referrals and rescheduling: She may refer discovery motions to a magistrate judge and will refer settlement conferences or mediation on request, by contacting chambers or filing a motion. Ask to reschedule any proceeding, including a phone conference, by motion that offers three alternative dates when all counsel are available, and states the other side’s position if it isn’t a joint motion.

docs.t: Judge Kari A. Dooley (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Kari A. Dooley, D. Conn.. Trial: Jury selection is generally the first Tuesday of each month, and jury trials run Monday to Friday. Lawyers arrive by 9:00 a.m. and jurors by 9:30. She prefers to release jurors around 4:45 p.m. but may keep them later to avoid bringing a witness back. She disfavors openings: you must ask permission. She sets closing limits with counsel and no time limits on the trial or witnesses. Pre-mark exhibits numerically: plaintiff’s from 1, defendant’s from 500, with counsel coordinating when there are several parties. The exhibit list describes each exhibit and says whether anyone objects and why. Confer on which are marked full and which for identification. She prefers one paper copy of all pre-marked exhibits before a hearing or trial, though day-of delivery is fine. Her courtroom is electronic, and she prefers exhibits shown electronically. Ask the courtr

docs.t: Judge Kari A. Dooley (D. Conn.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Kari A. Dooley, D. Conn.. Criminal cases: She doesn’t refer pleas to a magistrate judge, and sets a presentencing briefing schedule when sentencing is scheduled. Tell her early if sentencing needs an evidentiary hearing. She usually refers bond and release motions to the magistrate judge who held the detention hearing, and a proposed bond package goes to Probation at least 48 hours before the hearing. For an emergency motion, also call chambers. An initial jury selection and trial date are set at arraignment, followed by a phone status conference where she expects defense counsel to have discussed the Speedy Trial Act with the client. In her criminal cases the government’s exhibits start at 1 and the defendant’s at 500. For identifiable victims, she asks the government or a victim representative at covered proceedings whether the victim was notified and wants to be heard.

docs.t: Judge Sarala V. Nagala (D. Conn.) — Communications with the court
docs.x: Judge Sarala V. Nagala, D. Conn.. Communications with the court: She doesn’t read letters from parties, whether addressed to her or the Clerk, and has the Clerk return them. To ask for anything, file a motion for specific relief or a notice of specific information, captioned and following the Local Rules (especially Rule 7). Only compliant motions and notices are docketed and reviewed. An email to chambers for logistical questions must copy all counsel or parties. She won’t accept ex parte email.

docs.t: Judge Sarala V. Nagala (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and discovery period
docs.x: Judge Sarala V. Nagala, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and discovery period: She treats the report as critical, and her courtroom deputy generates a notice if it is late. It should give a meaningful overview of the claims and defenses, settlement possibilities, and the discovery you want. She decides for herself whether to hold a scheduling conference, taking into account whether you asked for one. If your deadlines are reasonable, the report usually becomes the initial scheduling order. She prefers discovery to close six to nine months after the report is filed, and may enter a nine-month cutoff even if you ask for more unless you explain why. List actual deadline dates, even if they are tied to earlier events. She modifies a schedule only for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Sarala V. Nagala (D. Conn.) — Extensions
docs.x: Judge Sarala V. Nagala, D. Conn.. Extensions: File strictly under Local Rule 7(b): at least three business days ahead, with the other side’s position, the number of earlier extension motions for the same deadline, and particularized good cause. A non-compliant motion may be denied.

docs.t: Judge Sarala V. Nagala (D. Conn.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Sarala V. Nagala, D. Conn.. Discovery disputes: She may decide them herself or refer them to a magistrate judge. Even after briefing, she expects you to keep trying to resolve the dispute without the court.

docs.t: Judge Sarala V. Nagala (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies
docs.x: Judge Sarala V. Nagala, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies: Unless ordered otherwise, within three business days after e-filing in a civil case, deliver two paper copies, with all exhibits and attachments, of: TRO, preliminary-injunction and prejudgment-remedy applications and their papers; dispositive motions, supporting memoranda, oppositions and replies; proposed voir dire and jury instructions; joint trial memoranda; trial briefs with proposed findings and conclusions; any other motion-related filing over 25 pages; and any filing with significant color exhibits. Print from the docket with the ECF header, order and tab them, and use a three-ring binder if they can’t be stapled. Don’t send copies of brief routine procedural motions unless asked. docs.t: Judge Sarala V. Nagala (D. Conn.) — Letter briefs, sur-replies, and argument
docs.x: Judge Sarala V. Nagala, D. Conn.. Letter briefs, sur-replies, and argument: No letter briefs and no sur-replies. File a formal motion, or a notice of supplemental authority for new cases. She usually schedules argument on dispositive motions and gives strong weight to a request, but may rule without it. If you will use a PowerPoint or exhibits not already on the docket at argument, share them with opposing counsel at least 24 hours ahead, or you will generally be barred from using them. She welcomes junior lawyers arguing and may let a second senior lawyer argue for a party too. She ordinarily rules on dispositive motions in writing, and may rule orally from the bench after argument.

docs.t: Judge Sarala V. Nagala (D. Conn.) — Settlement
docs.x: Judge Sarala V. Nagala, D. Conn.. Settlement: Nearly all civil cases settle, and at some point she will refer the parties to a magistrate judge. Magistrate judges may not be available on short notice, so seek a referral early with a brief motion saying all counsel conferred and agree. She encourages limited early discovery before a formal settlement conference if it would help.

docs.t: Judge Sarala V. Nagala (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Sarala V. Nagala, D. Conn.. Trial: Jury selection is typically on the fourth Tuesday of each month, lasting a half day to a full day. A trial day runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with a 45-minute lunch and two 15-minute breaks, four or five days a week. Counsel report at 9:00 a.m. and may need to stay after the day ends to handle objections. Civil openings are short, closings generally up to an hour per side. In a criminal jury case, move for permission to open. Her Joint Trial Memorandum instructions control exhibits, and require motions in limine and proposed jury instructions to be filed with the memorandum. She drafts the charge, gives it to the parties during trial, and holds a charge conference a day or two before. State objections in as few words as possible, with no argument. No lawyer contact with jurors after the trial. Exhibits are usually shown through the court’s technology

docs.t: Judge Sarala V. Nagala (D. Conn.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Sarala V. Nagala, D. Conn.. Criminal cases: She typically refers bond and release motions to the magistrate judge who held the detention hearing. Whoever files a pretrial-release request must also email a copy to that magistrate judge’s courtroom deputy, and failing to do so may cause substantial delay. She sets a status conference within 21 days of arraignment where you should propose firm dates. She doesn’t generally refer pleas to a magistrate judge. Unless the scheduling order says otherwise, sentencing memoranda are due from the defense at least 14 days before sentencing, from the government at least 7 days before, and any defense reply at least 3 days before. Tell her early if sentencing needs an evidentiary hearing. She asks the government at covered proceedings whether victims were notified and want to be heard.

docs.t: Judge Janet C. Hall (D. Conn.) — Argument and rulings
docs.x: Judge Janet C. Hall, D. Conn.. Argument and rulings: She hears argument on dispositive motions if she has questions, never by telephone, and has no motion day. A request for argument doesn’t change when she decides. She occasionally rules from the bench. She invites junior lawyers to argue and may allow a second senior lawyer to supplement.

docs.t: Judge Janet C. Hall (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report
docs.x: Judge Janet C. Hall, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report: Reports must give actual deadline dates. Dates tied to earlier events are not acceptable. She issues her final pretrial order with the 26(f) order, similar to but not identical to the standing order.

docs.t: Judge Janet C. Hall (D. Conn.) — Briefs and extensions
docs.x: Judge Janet C. Hall, D. Conn.. Briefs and extensions: Any briefing beyond motion, response and reply needs a motion for permission, and she is skeptical of it given her use of argument. She doesn’t favor letter briefs: file a formal motion, or a notice of supplemental authority for new cases. For urgent motions, file with the Clerk and send chambers a copy with a short cover letter. Extension requests by telephone are never granted. For an expedited ruling on an extension motion, send a courtesy copy and cover letter. Reconsideration motions must follow Local Rule 7(c). Lawyer affidavits aren’t needed to identify exhibits and transcripts on dispositive motions.

docs.t: Judge Janet C. Hall (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies
docs.x: Judge Janet C. Hall, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies: Unless ordered otherwise, on the next business day after e-filing, deliver one paper copy with the CM/ECF header on every page of: TRO, preliminary-injunction and prejudgment-remedy applications; dispositive motions; requested jury instructions; compliance with pretrial orders; trial briefs with proposed findings and conclusions; and any other motion or request that, with its related filings, runs over 20 pages.

docs.t: Judge Janet C. Hall (D. Conn.) — Referrals and settlement
docs.x: Judge Janet C. Hall, D. Conn.. Referrals and settlement: She doesn’t refer dispositive motions to magistrate judges. She refers settlement conferences and sometimes case management by random assignment, and occasionally discovery disputes, though she prefers to resolve those herself when time permits (some go to Magistrate Judge Merriam). She also refers to parajudicial officers or special masters on request. Pre-filing conferences aren’t required. For TROs and preliminary injunctions an order to show cause and proposed order help, and say clearly whether you want ex parte relief, an immediate hearing, or something else.

docs.t: Judge Janet C. Hall (D. Conn.) — Joint trial memorandum and exhibits
docs.x: Judge Janet C. Hall, D. Conn.. Joint trial memorandum and exhibits: After the dispositive-motion deadline passes or a ruling issues, she generally puts the case on a trial-ready calendar call, where she sets final deadlines and makes referrals. File motions in limine with the pretrial memorandum, and Daubert motions no later than the dispositive-motion deadline, or they are waived. Counsel must try to stipulate to uncontroversial facts and agree on a statement of the contested issues of fact and law. Submit proposed findings or jury instructions on diskette in Word format. Mark exhibits numerically and exchange copies at least seven calendar days before filing the pretrial memoranda. Submit the originals and a set of copies to the deputy clerk three calendar days before the pretrial conference. File objections other than relevance at least seven days before the conference, and evidentiar

docs.t: Judge Janet C. Hall (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Janet C. Hall, D. Conn.. Trial: Typical hours are 9:30 a.m. to 3:45 p.m. with a 45-minute lunch and one morning break, five days a week. Long cases may run 9:00 to 5:00 four days a week. She usually sets no time limits. Civil openings must be non-argumentative and are typically five minutes or less, and closings generally 30 minutes. Disclose demonstratives in advance. They can’t be used in closing unless marked as an exhibit or shared at least a day earlier. She rarely permits sidebars and doesn’t excuse the jury for motions. Objections must be short and cite a rule or brief ground, with no argument. She uses the strike method in civil cases and asks counsel to identify all attorneys in a local office only. A civil jury is typically eight for a week or less and ten to twelve for longer, and all deliberate. Jurors take notes and counsel may give them exhibit notebooks. She sends a

docs.t: Judge Sarah F. Russell (D. Conn.) — Communications with the court
docs.x: Judge Sarah F. Russell, D. Conn.. Communications with the court: She doesn’t review letters from parties, whether addressed to her or the Clerk, and has the Clerk return them. To ask for anything, file a motion for specific relief or a notice of specific information, captioned and following the Local Rules (especially Rule 7). Only compliant filings are docketed and reviewed.

docs.t: Judge Sarah F. Russell (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and discovery period
docs.x: Judge Sarah F. Russell, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and discovery period: She treats the report as critical, and her courtroom deputy generates a notice if it is late. It should give a meaningful overview, and she decides for herself whether a scheduling conference is needed, considering whether you asked for one. If your deadlines are reasonable, it usually becomes the scheduling order. She prefers discovery to close six to nine months after the report is filed, and may enter a nine-month cutoff even if you ask for more unless you explain why. Include actual deadline dates, even if tied to earlier events. She modifies a schedule only for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Sarah F. Russell (D. Conn.) — Extensions
docs.x: Judge Sarah F. Russell, D. Conn.. Extensions: File strictly under Local Rule 7(b): three business days ahead, the other side’s position, the number of earlier extension motions, and particularized good cause. Also state the specific date you want. A non-compliant motion may be denied.

docs.t: Judge Sarah F. Russell (D. Conn.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Sarah F. Russell, D. Conn.. Discovery: She may decide disputes herself or refer them to a magistrate judge, and expects you to keep trying to resolve them even after briefing.

docs.t: Judge Sarah F. Russell (D. Conn.) — Chambers’ copies
docs.x: Judge Sarah F. Russell, D. Conn.. Chambers’ copies: Unless ordered otherwise, within three business days after e-filing in a civil case, deliver two paper copies, with all exhibits and attachments, of: TRO, preliminary-injunction and prejudgment-remedy applications; dispositive motions, supporting memoranda, oppositions and replies; proposed voir dire and jury instructions; joint trial memoranda; trial briefs with proposed findings and conclusions; any other motion-related filing over 25 pages; and any filing with significant color exhibits. Print from the docket with the ECF header, order and tab, and use a three-ring binder if they can’t be stapled. Skip brief routine procedural motions unless asked. Mail or courier copies go to Chambers of the Hon. Sarah F. Russell at 141 Church Street, New Haven. Hand-delivered copies go c/o the Clerk’s Office at the same address.

docs.t: Judge Sarah F. Russell (D. Conn.) — Letter briefs, sur-replies, and argument
docs.x: Judge Sarah F. Russell, D. Conn.. Letter briefs, sur-replies, and argument: No letter briefs and no sur-replies. File a formal motion, or a notice of supplemental authority for new cases. She often schedules argument on dispositive motions and gives strong weight to a request, but may rule without it. A PowerPoint or exhibits not already on the docket must be shared with opposing counsel at least 24 hours before argument, or you will generally be barred from using them. She invites junior lawyers to argue and may allow a second senior lawyer to argue for a party too.

docs.t: Judge Sarah F. Russell (D. Conn.) — Settlement
docs.x: Judge Sarah F. Russell, D. Conn.. Settlement: Nearly all civil cases settle, and at some point she will refer the parties to a magistrate judge. Magistrate judges may not be available on short notice, so seek a referral early with a brief motion saying all counsel conferred and agree. She encourages limited early discovery before a formal conference if it would help.

docs.t: Judge Sarah F. Russell (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Sarah F. Russell, D. Conn.. Trial: Jury selection is generally the second Tuesday of each month. A trial day runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with a 45-minute lunch and two 15-minute breaks, four or five days a week. Counsel report at 9:00 a.m. and may need to stay late for objections. Civil openings are short, and closing limits are set with counsel. In a criminal jury case, move for permission to open. Agree in advance on exhibits admissible without foundation. Disclose demonstratives beforehand, and they can’t be used in closing unless marked as an exhibit or shared at least a day earlier. Her Joint Trial Memorandum instructions control exhibits, and require motions in limine and proposed jury instructions with the memorandum. State objections in a few words with no argument. She drafts the charge, shares it during trial, and holds a charge conference a day or two before. No lawyer c

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Communicating with chambers
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Communicating with chambers: He wants case-related questions handled through the docket, not by phone or email to chambers, and doesn’t accept informal letters from anyone. The Clerk returns them unread.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and discovery period
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and discovery period: He treats the report as critical and values one that outlines the main issues and flags likely discovery disputes. He decides for himself whether to hold a scheduling conference, considering your request. He generally defers to reasonable deadlines you propose and uses them in the initial scheduling order, but expects discovery to close six to nine months after the report is filed. He may enter a nine-month cutoff even if you ask for more unless you explain why. He modifies a schedule only for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Courtesy copies: Unless ordered otherwise, within three business days after e-filing, deliver two paper copies of any filing over 20 pages, with all exhibits and attachments, to the Clerk’s office to his attention. Print double-sided when possible, from the docket with the ECF header, ordered and tabbed, and use a three-ring binder if they can’t be stapled. Don’t send brief routine procedural motions unless asked.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Motions: He doesn’t require a pre-filing conference for dispositive motions. Extension and adjournment requests under Local Rule 7(b) must state the original date, the number of earlier requests, whether they were granted or denied, and whether the other side consents. If it doesn’t, give its stated reasons. A motion to withdraw as counsel must show the client had actual notice, or it will be denied. He decides case by case whether to hear argument, may rule from the bench, and says briefing quality affects how fast he can rule. He welcomes junior lawyers arguing and may hear supplemental argument from senior counsel.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Discovery and settlement
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Discovery and settlement: He prefers to refer discovery disputes to a magistrate judge. He refers settlement conferences to a magistrate judge. If the parties agree one would help, file a joint request asking for the referral, and prepare well for it.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Trial: His trial preferences are in his Joint Trial Memorandum Instructions and his standing order on jury selection, which we did not read. Read both before you prepare a pretrial filing.

docs.t: Judge Miranda Du (D. Nev.) — Communications and copies
docs.x: Judge Miranda Du, D. Nev.. Communications and copies: She keeps a paperless chambers: don’t send courtesy copies unless she asks. File searchable PDFs under LR IC 2-2 and LR IA 10-1. Counsel are strongly discouraged from contacting chambers directly about case matters except as LR IA 7-1(a) allows. Use the standing order, or ask the courtroom deputy or Clerk’s office. Filings that don’t follow the Local Rules or her order may be stricken.

docs.t: Judge Miranda Du (D. Nev.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Miranda Du, D. Nev.. Motions: She decides jurisdictional motions, such as remand or lack of personal or subject-matter jurisdiction, before other motions, to avoid needless discovery. Otherwise motions are decided in the order filed unless one needs expedited treatment. Submit a proposed order, attached as an exhibit, with every stipulation and unopposed motion, including a motion for default judgment. When she grants a stay, any pending motions are automatically denied without prejudice, and a party may move to reinstate them when the stay lifts. File one consolidated motion in limine rather than separate motions on single issues.

docs.t: Judge Miranda Du (D. Nev.) — Trial and settlement
docs.x: Judge Miranda Du, D. Nev.. Trial and settlement: Trial is set after the settlement conference, or after the joint pretrial order if the case doesn’t settle, on the first available trial stack. Her standard Order Regarding Trial is filed once a trial is scheduled. A case usually goes to the assigned magistrate judge for a settlement conference after dispositive motions are decided, or as soon as the joint pretrial order is filed if there are none. Electronic devices are allowed for calendars and for presenting evidence or argument, but not devices that cause feedback or interfere with the court recording equipment. She strongly encourages lead counsel to let newer lawyers argue, examine witnesses and play a real role.

docs.t: Judge Andrew P. Gordon (D. Nev.) — Courtesy copies and proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Andrew P. Gordon, D. Nev.. Courtesy copies and proposed orders: Don’t deliver paper courtesy copies unless chambers asks. If asked, bind them and tab the exhibits. Submit a proposed order with every stipulation and unopposed motion, including default judgment. It can be an exhibit or a separate filing, and must also be emailed in Word format to his chambers address.

docs.t: Judge Andrew P. Gordon (D. Nev.) — Hearings and junior lawyers
docs.x: Judge Andrew P. Gordon, D. Nev.. Hearings and junior lawyers: Motions may be decided with or without a hearing under LR 78-1. Add a note in the filing, or a separate notice, that a lawyer with six or fewer years of experience will argue. If he is inclined to rule on the papers, that representation weighs in favor of holding argument. He will entertain a reasonable request for a senior lawyer to supplement the junior lawyer’s argument. He generally grants requests to appear by phone or video for just cause.

docs.t: Judge Andrew P. Gordon (D. Nev.) — Staff, transcripts and technology
docs.x: Judge Andrew P. Gordon, D. Nev.. Staff, transcripts and technology: Court staff may contact counsel about scheduling or trial status, and he strongly urges a prompt response. For expedited or daily transcripts, contact the court reporter as early as possible, because advance deposits likely will be required and a late request may be refused. Phones, iPads, laptops and printers are allowed to check calendars and present evidence or argument, but must be off until the judge permits. Use the courtroom’s presentation resources. Training is arranged through his courtroom administrator.

docs.t: Judge Andrew P. Gordon (D. Nev.) — Settlement, trial dates and jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Andrew P. Gordon, D. Nev.. Settlement, trial dates and jury instructions: Civil cases usually go to the assigned magistrate judge for a settlement conference after the joint pretrial order is filed. You may ask in writing for an early settlement or pretrial conference under LR 16-2. Trial is scheduled after the joint pretrial order on the first available trial stack. His Order Regarding Trial is filed shortly before trial, and a sample is on his page. He has stock jury instructions drawn from the Ninth Circuit’s model instructions, posted on his page. Your proposed instructions need not repeat them unless you disagree with one. They must be concise, understandable and neutral, and argumentative instructions will not be given.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Courtesy copies, calls and PDFs
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Courtesy copies, calls and PDFs: Paperless chambers: no courtesy copies unless requested. For docketing, scheduling and calendar matters, call the courtroom administrator. Calls to chambers are only for urgent matters. File searchable PDFs under LR IC 2-2 and LR IA 10-1. He appreciates OCR on exhibits too, though the rules don’t require it.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Motions: Non-dispositive motions may be referred to the magistrate judge. Jurisdictional motions, such as remand or lack of personal or subject-matter jurisdiction, are decided before other motions. Submit a proposed order with every stipulation and unopposed motion, including default judgment. He will consider a stipulation or motion for a continuance or extension filed at least three days before the deadline. Later requests are granted only in extraordinary circumstances with just cause. When a stay is granted, pending motions are automatically denied without prejudice, and a party may move to reinstate them. Hearings aren’t scheduled automatically. Put “(Hearing Requested)” on the front page directly under the title of the motion, response or reply.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Appearances, transcripts and technology
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Appearances, transcripts and technology: He will consider a request to appear by phone or video for just cause. Notify the court reporter immediately on receiving his order if you need expedited or daily transcripts. Cell phones must be off while court is in session, and recording court proceedings is strictly prohibited. Phones, iPads, laptops and printers are allowed for calendars and presenting evidence, but not devices that cause feedback or interfere with recording equipment.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Settlement and trial dates
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Settlement and trial dates: A case is usually referred to the magistrate judge for a settlement conference under LR 16-5 after dispositive motions are fully briefed. He will usually stay the ruling until the conference has happened. With no dispositive motions, referral comes as soon as the joint pretrial order is filed. You may ask in writing for an early pretrial conference under LR 16-2. Trial is scheduled after the settlement conference, or at the close of discovery. He rules on dispositive motions before the trial date. His Order Regarding Trial is filed as soon as trial is scheduled.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Joint pretrial order and trial procedures
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Joint pretrial order and trial procedures: Unless ordered otherwise, file a proposed joint pretrial order within 30 days after discovery closes. It must include the caption, trial counsel, jurisdiction statements, claims and defenses to be tried, trial days needed and jury or non-jury, whether all parties consented to a magistrate judge (without saying who did not), stipulations, witness list with summaries, deposition designations and objections, and an exhibit list. Mark one star for exhibits no one challenges on authenticity and two stars for exhibits no one objects to on any ground. Also file motions in limine, a pretrial memorandum if useful, requests to charge and proposed voir dire in jury cases, and proposed findings and conclusions in non-jury cases. docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Default judgment procedure
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Default judgment procedure: Prepare an order to show cause with the date and time of the conference left blank. File it with an attorney’s affidavit covering the basis for default, service, procedural history, whether default can be entered against fewer than all defendants, proposed damages and their basis, and why an inquest would be needed. Include a proposed default judgment, copies of all pleadings, the affidavit of service, and a Clerk’s certificate that no answer was filed if that is the basis. After he signs the order, serve the defendant with a conforming copy and the papers and file an affidavit of service before the signed order is filed.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Communications, copies and PDFs
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Communications, copies and PDFs: Counsel and parties are strongly discouraged from contacting chambers directly about case matters except as LR IA 7-1(a) allows. Call the Clerk’s Office or her courtroom administrator. She keeps a paperless chambers: no courtesy copies unless requested. File searchable PDFs under LR IC 2-2(a)(1). She appreciates OCR on exhibits too. Cell phones must be off in court, and recording is prohibited under General Order 2022-06.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Motions: Non-dispositive motions generally go to the magistrate judge. Jurisdictional motions are generally decided first. Submit a proposed order with every stipulation and unopposed motion, including default judgment. She will generally deny a stipulation or motion for extension or continuance that lacks justification. When a stay is granted, pending motions are automatically denied without prejudice, and additional briefing on reinstatement needs leave of court.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Motions to seal and pro hac vice
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Motions to seal and pro hac vice: A motion to seal must comply with LR IA 10-5 and also state whether the compelling-reasons or good-cause standard applies and explain, with specificity, why the public’s right of access is outweighed, citing Center for Auto Safety v. Chrysler and Kamakana. Failure to explain may mean denial. A pro hac vice petition must follow LR IA 11-1. Attach certificates of good standing issued within six months before filing from every state or territory where the lawyer is admitted. Signatures are needed from the petitioning attorney, local counsel and the party. A non-compliant petition may be denied and the petitioner required to repay the filing fee.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Hearings and remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Hearings and remote appearances: Hearings aren’t scheduled automatically. Put “(Hearing Requested)” on the front page under the title of the motion, response or reply. Motions are generally resolved without a hearing if no just cause is shown. Adding “Junior Attorney” under “Hearing Requested” makes a hearing more likely. File requests for phone or video appearances on the docket, no later than two business days before the hearing.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Settlement, trial dates and transcripts
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Settlement, trial dates and transcripts: A case usually goes to the magistrate judge for a settlement conference under LR 16-5, and she usually stays the ruling on dispositive motions until it happens. With no dispositive motions, referral comes once the joint pretrial order is filed. You may ask for an early pretrial conference under LR 16-2, and an alternate magistrate judge will preside. Trial is set after the settlement conference using the dates in your Joint Status Report or Joint Pretrial Order, and she rules on dispositive motions first. Her Order Regarding Trial is filed as soon as trial is scheduled. For expedited or daily transcripts, submit the AO 435 form by email to the court’s transcript address. Advance deposits are likely and a late request may be refused.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Filing
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Filing: File everything on CM/ECF. Pro se parties are exempt, but counsel in a case with a pro se party must still e-file. Proposed orders for stipulations, unopposed motions and default judgments, and jury instructions, are filed on ECF, and chambers may ask for a Word copy by email. No courtesy copies unless requested. Unsearchable PDFs may be rejected. LR IC 2-2 and IA 10-3 require an index of exhibits, a descriptive cover sheet on each exhibit (not just “Exhibit A”), and each exhibit as a separate file. Violations can lead to denial of the motion without prejudice.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Emergency motions and sealing
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Emergency motions and sealing: Emergency motions should be rare under LR 7-4(b) and need a declaration signed by counsel. A motion to seal must follow Center for Auto Safety v. Chrysler and state the legal standard and the reasons, the legitimate interest, the injury if sealing is denied and why a less restrictive option fails. It needs sworn evidence where necessary and a narrowly tailored proposed order that lists each document or portion to be sealed in a table. Explore alternatives, minimize sealing, and redact instead of sealing whole documents. Non-compliance means denial.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Communications with chambers
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Communications with chambers: All communications must be in writing and filed on ECF, with copies delivered to any parties who don’t get ECF notice. Don’t send her copies of correspondence between counsel. Call the courtroom deputy for docketing, scheduling or calendar questions. Ex parte calls about the substance of a case are prohibited. If a submission needs immediate attention, phone chambers after filing on ECF. Respond promptly if chambers staff contact you.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Argument, appearances and stays
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Argument, appearances and stays: Motions may be decided with or without a hearing under LR 78-1. Note in the filing, or in a separate notice, that a lawyer with six or fewer years of experience will argue. That representation weighs in favor of argument when she is inclined to rule on the papers, and a senior lawyer may supplement. She generally grants requests to appear by phone or video for just cause. A granted stay automatically denies pending motions without prejudice, and a party may move to reinstate them.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Motions in limine
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Motions in limine: File a single consolidated motion in limine, after meeting and conferring under LR 16-3(a). Each side is limited to 10 motions in limine of 10 pages each, even with several plaintiffs or defendants, who must coordinate. Replies are discouraged.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Settlement, trial and transcripts
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Settlement, trial and transcripts: Civil cases generally go to the magistrate judge for a settlement conference after the joint pretrial order is filed. You may ask for an early settlement or pretrial conference under LR 16-2. Trial is set after the joint pretrial order on the first available trial stack. She encourages consent to trial by a magistrate judge under LR IB 2-2. Her Order Regarding Trial is filed shortly before trial. Devices that cause feedback or interfere with recording equipment aren’t allowed in court. Contact the court reporter early for expedited or daily transcripts, because advance deposits will likely be required.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Pro se litigants and habeas
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Pro se litigants and habeas: Pro se litigants must communicate with the court only in writing and keep their contact information current, or risk dismissal or default under LR IA 3-1. Counsel dealing with a pro se party must follow the Nevada Rules of Professional Conduct on unrepresented persons. In habeas cases with pro se petitioners, the respondent must serve the petitioner with the answer and the record when filing them, and the record must include a table of contents or index.

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Hearings, copies and filing
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Hearings, copies and filing: He decides motions with or without a hearing under LR 78-1. If he orders one, his courtroom deputy will contact you, and if you don’t respond within 48 hours the court will set a time convenient to itself. Hearings and conferences are audio recorded and court reporters are usually not provided. Don’t submit paper courtesy copies unless requested. File searchable PDFs, and file each exhibit as a separate file, not part of the base document. Motions to seal must follow LR IA 10-5. A motion for leave to amend must follow LR 15-1 and also attach a redlined or highlighted comparison to the prior operative pleading.

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Case management: After an answer, he generally orders an initial Joint Case Management Report, which you must draft by meeting and conferring and must follow strictly. He may set a case management conference that lead counsel must attend. For any later conference, each party files its own report at least 5 court days before it, no longer than 10 double-spaced pages. It covers discovery completed, discovery served but not answered, and unresolved discovery issues with the meet-and-confer efforts and the resolution each side wants. Attach nothing except the relevant discovery excerpts, privilege logs or deposition testimony.

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Motions to dismiss and discovery
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Motions to dismiss and discovery: A motion to dismiss does not stay discovery. To stay discovery, file a motion that addresses the factors in Kor Media Group v. Green. A stay isn’t granted merely because a motion to dismiss is pending.

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Informal discovery dispute procedure
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Informal discovery dispute procedure: No discovery motion may be filed until you follow this procedure and he orders briefing. Lead counsel must first meet and confer in person, by video or by telephone. Letters, emails or a brief call don’t count. If that fails, the party seeking or resisting the discovery files a “Motion Regarding Discovery Dispute” of no more than 5 pages in 12-point type with one-inch margins. The only exhibits allowed are a declaration detailing the meet-and-confer (what was discussed on each request, concessions, and what was resolved) and a single exhibit reproducing only the disputed requests and responses. It must have separate sections for the unresolved issues, the party’s position with support, and the compromise it proposes. The opposing party files a response within 2 court days, also 5 pages, on the same terms. He then decid

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Emergency discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Emergency discovery disputes: During a deposition, after trying in good faith to resolve it, you may seek help under LR 37-1(b) by contacting his courtroom deputy or chambers. Before you do, email a short description of the dispute to his chambers address. If he is unavailable, the deposition continues with objections noted for the record.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Contacting chambers
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Contacting chambers: No letters in place of opposed extension requests, contested discovery, or substantive motions. Don’t copy her on letters to opposing counsel, and don’t send faxes or email. She permits no ex parte contact. Don’t call chambers with questions the rules answer. Case questions go to the courtroom deputy. Counsel may not communicate directly with her law clerks, and a clerk who contacts you does so at her direction. Read each order itself, because the docket description is sometimes inaccurate.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Argument and conferences
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Argument and conferences: She sets no regular days for argument or evidentiary hearings and schedules them ad hoc. She hears argument if it will help, and a party may ask in writing. She may hold telephone conferences on scheduling and motions and usually asks counsel to place the call. Bring matters to her only after discussing them with opposing counsel.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Motions, replies, and orders
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Motions, replies, and orders: Motion practice follows LR 7.3. She strongly urges following LR 7.6 on evidentiary objections. Absent leave and good cause, no reply or sur-reply may exceed ten pages. File a proposed order with every motion and response except dispositive motions, in Word or WordPerfect to her ECF mailbox. Title it “Order,” with no lawyer’s name, address, or client number. She is extremely reluctant to grant continuances, especially when counsel haven’t been diligent, but will consider good cause.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Working copies: Unless directed otherwise, deliver bound, tabbed copies to the Clerk’s Office within three days of filing injunctive-relief papers and any dispositive motion, brief, response, or reply that has an appendix or tabs. Courtesy copies of other motions are discouraged.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Summary judgment: Every summary judgment motion and opposition must recite the facts with complete, accurate record citations. She won’t consider any fact not supported by a citation. Give pinpoint cites such as the document title, a deponent’s name and pages, or an affidavit’s paragraph. Non-compliant papers may be stricken.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Settlement and injunctions
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Settlement and injunctions: She usually conducts settlement conferences in jury cases, and may refer a matter to the magistrate judge. Bench-trial cases are automatically referred. For a TRO she schedules a conference as soon as counsel have appeared, requires all counsel to be present unless urgency precludes notice, and rarely grants ex parte TROs. She combines preliminary and permanent injunction hearings when appropriate and usually allows expedited discovery. Proposed findings and conclusions are required in injunction cases.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Pretrial submissions
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Pretrial submissions: About three weeks before trial, the parties submit jointly proposed voir dire, jury instructions, and a verdict sheet, plus motions in limine and trial briefs. Send two copies of points for charge in an editable format. Where you disagree, give each side’s version and rationale. Responses to motions in limine are due within five business days, and no reply is allowed. She usually holds the final pretrial conference about two weeks before trial.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Trial: Court convenes promptly at 9:30 a.m. and may sit until 5:00 or later. She conducts voir dire herself, and counsel submit proposed questions at least five business days before trial. Mark and exchange exhibits before trial and give her two copies in binders with a schedule describing each. No speaking objections, and no continuing objections: state the basis in a word or phrase. Only one lawyer per party may examine a witness. Jurors take notes. She gives counsel her final jury instructions before trial. Counsel must stay within five minutes of the courthouse during deliberations. No food, including bottled water, in the courtroom.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Criminal cases: Follow the term’s scheduling order. Request extensions and continuances well before the term starts under LR 6.1. Submit proposed plea agreements and factual basis documents two business days before the plea hearing if not filed under the schedule, or the case is removed from the calendar. File sentencing memoranda at least two full business days before sentencing. A joint request to change the guideline calculation after the final presentence report must be filed at least three full business days before. File requests for departures and variances at least three business days before sentencing.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Chambers
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Chambers: Your point of contact is the courtroom deputy clerk, by email or in writing. Don’t discuss the merits with her or the law clerks, and they won’t say when a ruling will issue.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — AI certification
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. AI certification: Certify at the end of every filing either that no generative AI was used, including in research, or that anything AI influenced was personally reviewed for accuracy and every citation is to a real authority that says what you claim. The certification doesn’t count against page limits, and a filing without it may be stricken without leave to amend.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Diversity jurisdiction
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Diversity jurisdiction: Plead citizenship affirmatively and distinctly. Alleging a party is not a citizen of a state, or only where an individual resides, isn’t enough. For LLCs and other unincorporated entities, name every member and trace citizenship through every layer, and an estate takes the decedent’s citizenship.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Filing basics
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Filing basics: All filings must be text-searchable. A TRO or preliminary injunction request must be made by motion, and a request for expedited consideration must also be emailed to the courtroom deputy. File a proposed order with every motion. Cite the record by docket entry number and CM/ECF page, in the body of the brief and not in footnotes.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Extensions
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Extensions: Extensions, including of discovery deadlines, are granted generally only if you couldn’t reasonably have anticipated the need. Ask promptly, say whether the other side consents, and give a specific timetable. He generally won’t extend page limits, and a request must come at least five days before the deadline.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Discovery disputes: Meet and confer by phone or in person, since letters or email don’t satisfy it unless repeated attempts fail through the adversary’s conduct. If unresolved, file a Joint Statement Regarding Discovery Dispute of three single-spaced pages with the disputed requests attached and a certificate of conferral. He then decides whether to rule on the papers or hold a recorded conference. You need his permission through this process before filing any motion to compel, quash, for a protective order, or for sanctions. All discovery must be initiated so responses are due before the close of discovery, and he won’t enforce side agreements to go past it.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Sealing and experts
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Sealing and experts: He strongly disfavors motions to seal. Protective orders must contain his required sealing language and follow Local Rules Appendix H II(J). Don’t file a motion to exclude expert testimony until after summary judgment unless needed to resolve it.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Motions generally
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Motions generally: Meet and confer before any dispositive motion and certify that you did. Multiple plaintiffs or defendants file one consolidated dispositive motion and one objection to a report and recommendation absent leave. State and develop each argument in the body with particular authority, since he may disregard arguments in footnotes, incorporated by reference, or raised first in a reply.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Failing to respond
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Failing to respond: Under his order, failing to respond timely to any motion is treated as consent and intentional abandonment, and he may grant the motion on that ground alone, even with prejudice. Failing to address part of a motion in a timely response is treated the same way for that part.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Summary judgment: He requires strict Local Rule 56.1 practice: a separate statement with one fact per numbered paragraph, a response that must be an admission, a direct refutation with pincites, or one of the listed objections, with the movant’s fact copied before each response, and a separate reply to refuting facts. He may disregard a whole paragraph or filing for one defect and deem facts admitted. A “no evidence” argument isn’t enough for a movant without the burden.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Argument, settlements, exhibits
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Argument, settlements, exhibits: Oral argument is more likely if a lawyer under five years out of law school will lead it. He won’t approve an FLSA settlement that bars the plaintiff from disclosing the claims or their resolution. Give him and his law clerk each a courtesy copy of any exhibit or demonstrative introduced in court.

The proposed pretrial order is due 7 days before the pretrial conference, and dispositive motions are due 120 days before it.
