docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Hearings and remote appearances
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Hearings and remote appearances: Courtroom 1, 3rd floor, Moakley Courthouse, Boston. (The undated trial instructions refer to Courtroom 2 as the judge’s electronic courtroom; the page lists Courtroom 1.) Civil motion hearings are normally by Zoom if either counsel is from out of state or must travel a considerable distance. Most civil status conferences are by telephone, with Zoom for complex or multi-party cases; criminal status conferences are by Zoom, and some pleas by video for good reason, though in-court appearances are preferred. Under the 2014 telephone order, ask the courtroom clerk for permission to appear by phone early enough to appear in person if refused. Call from a normal office setting, avoid cell phones, never from a moving car or a noisy public place, and identify yourself each time you speak.

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Motions and briefing (trap)
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Motions and briefing (trap): A reply needs no leave if it is no more than 12 pages, double-spaced, and filed within 7 days (excluding intermediate weekends and legal holidays) after service of the opposition. Longer replies need good cause; surreplies need leave, usually granted on request, and the proposed brief may be filed with the motion for leave. Under the 2023 scheduling-order template, oppositions to dispositive motions are due within 21 days after service. Motions to dismiss and for summary judgment are heard, with no time limits beyond “good sense and common courtesy.” Post-argument briefs may be allowed where the hearing raised issues not fully developed. Courtesy copies are not required for dispositive motions, though helpful when the file is voluminous.

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Scheduling and case management
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Scheduling and case management: The clerk issues a Notice of Scheduling Conference with a scheduling-order template. The judge sets fact and expert discovery, amendment, motion, and status-conference dates; status conferences come at least after the close of fact discovery, usually also about two-thirds through it, and monthly in very complicated cases. If expert testimony seems unlikely, the order omits expert discovery but sets a deadline to file a notice of intent to call an expert; filing one resets the calendar. Motions to extend must state the reasons, summarize the discovery remaining, and give a specific completion date; they are granted only for good cause. Lead trial counsel must attend the initial, final, and any interim pretrial conferences; other conferences may be handled by any prepared counsel. The pretrial memorandum under L.R. 16.5(d

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Discovery (trap)
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Discovery (trap): Discovery motions are typically referred to the magistrate judge; if kept, they are normally heard, and may be resolved at status conferences. Except for good cause, motions to compel, for protective orders, to quash, to strike discovery responses, and similar motions must be filed by the close of fact or expert discovery, whichever applies. Daubert deadlines are usually set later, at a status conference once counsel flag the issue; ideally hearings follow the close of expert discovery and come well before trial. ESI is addressed only if there is a dispute.

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Mediation: The judge refers a case to mediation only if both sides agree, will not force mediation or settlement talks, and expects parties who will not settle to litigate.

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Patent cases
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Patent cases: A separate scheduling template applies: patentee’s preliminary infringement disclosures and the accused infringer’s invalidity and non-infringement contentions, each amendable up to 30 days before the Markman hearing and afterward only by leave for good cause. Claim construction: simultaneous exchange of terms, then preliminary briefs (25 pages) and replies (15 pages), then a joint claim construction and prehearing statement that prioritizes and limits disputed terms, includes a joint chart, states hearing length and any witnesses, and proposes an order of argument. The judge generally favors tutorials in all but the simplest cases; tutorial materials in written or media form are exchanged 5 days before the hearing.

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Pretrial
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Pretrial: In a case of average complexity, proposed voir dire, jury instructions, verdict forms, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine are due about two weeks before trial; no special format or page limit. Motions in limine are heard at the final pretrial conference; Daubert motions are typically resolved well before it. Civil trial dates are set after the joint pretrial memorandum estimates trial length. Only the L.R. 16.5 joint pretrial memorandum is required, with trial briefs in complex cases. The initial pretrial conference covers logistics such as the daily schedule, evidence display, and empanelment.

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Trial (trap): Trial days run 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. sharp, with short breaks at 10:30 and noon (or one at 11); counsel meet the court at 8:30 a.m. daily. Exhibits get unique numbers only (no letters or letter-number combinations), marked “Exhibit,” not by party, with decimals for groups (13.1, 13.2). Numbers never change, and gaps are fine. Remove deposition-exhibit stickers, staple rather than clip, and avoid plastic sleeves. The judge strongly prefers a tabbed three-ring binder of exhibits by the morning of the first day. By the end of each trial day, tell opposing counsel the next day’s witnesses and a projection for the day after. Question from any reasonable spot but not next to the witness; approach without asking while acknowledging the court. Object with one word or a one- or two-word basis; argue at sidebar. Demonstratives are strongly preferred.

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Jury selection and charge
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Jury selection and charge: The court asks voir dire of the panel, then examines jurors one by one at sidebar; counsel may ask polite follow-up questions there. Peremptories are exercised at sidebar in alternating rounds with no back strikes. Civil trials seat 10 jurors; criminal trials seat 2 alternates, who are the last two seated and are not told until deliberations. Draft charges circulate during trial, with the final charge conference the afternoon before closings. Each juror gets a written charge, and counsel may quote the final charge in closing. Civil closings: plaintiff, defendant, plaintiff’s rebuttal (normally 5 or 10 minutes).

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Inexperienced attorneys
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Inexperienced attorneys: The judge strongly encourages relatively inexperienced attorneys to handle matters, including summary judgment arguments and trial examinations. They are held to full preparation standards, must have authority suited to the proceeding, and need supervision by a more experienced attorney for complex evidentiary work unless the court allows otherwise.

docs.t: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and sentencing
docs.x: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and sentencing: After referral back from the magistrate judge, the judge sees the parties at least every 30 days until the defendant decides to plead or go to trial, and sets a trial date when the defendant says the case will be tried. Release-condition motions involving new evidence or changed circumstances are normally referred to the magistrate judge; appeals are kept and detention reviews are heard. Sentencing memoranda are optional. Short continuances are granted for schedules; longer ones only in defined circumstances (e.g., RISE program or cooperation), never as informal probation.

docs.x: Judge Nina Morrison, E.D.N.Y.. Excerpts: Written submissions must be text-searchable to the extent practicable (except from pro se litigants). Submit proposed orders and certain documents by email in both PDF and Word to her chambers address, though you needn’t send Word files of stipulations of dismissal or settlement or of extension motions unless asked. Lawyers must enter a notice of appearance on ECF. She encourages less experienced and underrepresented attorneys to take part in court proceedings. If complying with her pre-motion practices would cost you a substantive right or a statutory deadline, you may file the motion on time with an explanation.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Case schedule (trap)
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Case schedule (trap): The judge follows L.R. 16.1 and sets a trial month at the initial scheduling conference, no more than 12 months out: summary judgment motions within 9 months, the final pretrial conference within 11 months, and trial within 12 months. Criminal trial dates are also set at the initial conference. No status conferences unless a party asks. The judge does not ask about settlement at the scheduling conference but schedules mediation unless the parties refuse.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Motions and hearings
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Motions and hearings: Motions to dismiss and summary judgment motions are heard, usually with no more than 10 minutes per side (5 for more straightforward motions). Replies and sur-replies are welcome with no page limit, as are post-argument briefs, but the judge does not wait for them before ruling. Provide a courtesy copy if exhibits are voluminous.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Discovery and sealing
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Discovery and sealing: The judge decides discovery motions personally, on the papers, with oral hearings only in extremely rare circumstances. Emergency motions are always considered, but “Calling a motion an emergency doesn’t make it one.” On proportionality and case management, the judge acts like a baseball arbitrator, choosing whichever party’s proposal is more reasonable and proportionate. Bifurcation is considered but usually causes delay. Filing under seal is disfavored, and a general protective order is not the place to provide for sealed filings.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Experts and Daubert (trap)
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Experts and Daubert (trap): No expert may testify to anything not fully revealed in the expert’s report. Daubert hearings are extremely rare. Daubert motions should be resolved before the close of discovery, so a different expert can be substituted if necessary.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Patent and Markman
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Patent and Markman: Patent cases are managed like any other case. About eight disputed constructions are enough for one case. The judge takes the bench with a tentative construction and discusses it with the parties; if either side is dissatisfied, the judge hears one expert per side in a one-hour “hot tub” session. Jointly agreed written tutorials are welcome.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Pretrial (trap)
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Pretrial (trap): Proposed voir dire, jury instructions, verdict forms, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine are due at the latest on the Friday before the Monday empanelment. Motions in limine are limited to 20 pages and are not heard at the final pretrial conference. No initial pretrial conference in civil cases. Trial briefs are welcome but not required, and the number of trial days is agreed at the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Trial: Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Openings are generally 15 minutes per side and closings 30 minutes per side, and the judge keeps time. Exhibits get numbers when admitted, regardless of which party offers them; exhibits for identification get letters A to Z, then AA, AB, AC (not AA, BB, CC). Advance courtesy copies of trial exhibits are welcome but not required. No podium requirement and no limit on rounds of examination (the rules of evidence govern). Tell the judge before using chalks; rebuttal cases should be rare. At bench trials, do not read depositions aloud; the judge reads them.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Jury selection and charge
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Jury selection and charge: The judge questions the venire, with no attorney voir dire, and has each seated juror describe their work. Peremptories alternate (plaintiff or prosecution first, then defense first in the next round), with no back strikes; the judge picks the foreperson. The judge seats 12 jurors in civil trials and 2 alternates in criminal trials. Questionnaires are used in high-publicity cases and should be short (preferably one page), focused on knowledge of the case and potential bias. At the charge conference the judge explains the proposed charge and discusses it. General verdicts are favored, though special verdict proposals are considered; the jury gets a written charge if deliberations go into a second day.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Criminal cases: The judge handles criminal discovery, usually on the papers, and refers release-condition motions to the magistrate judge, but holds hearings on detention reviews. Sentencing memoranda are welcome but not required; submit them in time to be read. Victim impact statements come early in the hearing, before the guideline calculation, argument, and allocution. Expedited sentencing is considered when the likely incarceration is shorter than the usual preparation time; postponement when it could favor the defendant and the government does not object.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Electronic filing
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Electronic filing: Under the May 6, 2026 standing order, anyone applying for electronic filing privileges must certify understanding of and ability to meet the requirements. Court staff may not e-file for anyone who has e-filing privileges; those unable to e-file may file on paper.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Briefing and motion hearings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Briefing and motion hearings (trap): Reply and surreply briefs are not allowed without leave of court for good cause, and are limited to 10 pages. No courtesy copies of dispositive-motion papers are required. Motions to dismiss are usually not heard (sometimes with the scheduling conference); summary judgment motions are heard only when issues are not sufficiently briefed. Argument is limited to 15 minutes per side, and post-argument briefs are allowed rarely. Patent cases follow Local Rule 16.6 and Appendix E; Markman hearings have time limits that counsel may use as they choose.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Discovery (trap)
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Discovery (trap): The judge regards most discovery motions as unnecessary, typically refers them to the magistrate judge without a hearing, and may sanction counsel found obstreperous or obstructive. Emergency discovery motions are considered only in rare circumstances. Any proposed protective order must confirm it is specifically subject to Local Rule 7.2. Bifurcated discovery is rare. Expert disclosures must comply with Rule 26(a)(2). All expert deadlines are set at the initial scheduling conference; Daubert motions are not scheduled, are rarely heard, are taken up earlier in the case; a large majority of those filed are denied.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Scheduling conference: The senior lawyers ultimately responsible for the case must attend and comply with Local Rule 16.1(B), (C), and (D); a continuance is given only if counsel is actually engaged on trial, and noncompliance may draw Local Rule 1.3 sanctions. Plaintiff’s counsel must notify parties who have not appeared. For Local Rule 16.1(D)(3) budget and ADR certifications, the survey says the judge prefers copies of litigants’ signatures to electronic signatures (originals not needed); the conference notice says electronic signatures are acceptable but filing certifies counsel hold actual signatures. The schedule is set for the entire case, through final pretrial conference and trial. Status conferences are not usual; mediation is encouraged after fact discovery but not required.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Remote appearances: No case events are routinely held by Zoom in civil or criminal cases; Zoom is considered for good cause shown. The judge reports no COVID-19 restrictions.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Pretrial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Pretrial (trap): There is no initial pretrial conference in civil or criminal cases. Deadlines are set at the pretrial conference; motions in limine (10-page limit), jury instruction requests, voir dire questions, and objections to the other side’s witness and exhibit lists are generally due 2 or 3 weeks before trial. The judge wants paper copies of proposed voir dire, verdict forms, and jury instructions in chambers. At the final pretrial conference the judge announces tentative rulings on motions in limine and lets counsel try to dissuade the court. Trial briefs are not required but are often helpful. Exhibits are premarked sequentially, with no separate government or defendant exhibits. No courtesy copies of trial exhibits.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Trial: Trial runs 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. and 2:00 to 3:30 p.m. Time limits are set at the final pretrial conference, and for closings at the charge conference. Counsel use a movable podium or none and may not wander the courtroom; sidebars only when absolutely necessary. Chalks are allowed subject to objection beforehand. Examination is direct, cross, redirect, and recross (further rounds rarely). Civil juries are 12; criminal trials usually have 2 alternates. The charge conference is held at or near the end of testimony, and the jury gets a written charge. Bench trials require proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law before trial; they may be supplemented after trial.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Jury selection: The court poses voir dire (as supplemented by counsel) to the sworn panel; jurors with affirmative answers are questioned at sidebar, where counsel may ask related questions. After a clean slate, the court asks each juror’s and spouse’s occupation, and peremptories are exercised alternately at sidebar with no back strikes. Questionnaires only in high-profile cases.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: All pretrial matters, criminal discovery, and release motions go to the magistrate judge. No hearing on review of detention orders; suppression motions are decided on the papers unless a hearing is warranted. Sentencing memoranda are not required but strongly advised. Expedited sentencing when the probation officer agrees; sentencing postponed only for very good cause. In revocation matters the judge asks counsel about Rule 32.1(b)(2).

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — CJA interim vouchers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. CJA interim vouchers (trap): No motion for interim excess compensation is needed, but absent leave CJA counsel must submit a first interim CJA 20 voucher once unpaid fees and expenses reach $19,000, with a memorandum explaining why the case is “extended” or “complex” and the excess compensation is needed. Further interim vouchers are due whenever unpaid amounts reach $9,000, with a memorandum that also summarizes prior interim payments (standing order, May 7, 2010).

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Trial schedule and courtroom
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Trial schedule and courtroom: Civil jury, non-jury, and criminal trials run 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. (jury trials on that schedule until deliberations), in Courtroom 1, 3rd floor, Moakley Courthouse, Boston. The “5 minute rule”: during jury deliberations counsel may leave the courtroom but must be back within 5 minutes of a call from the deputy clerk for a jury question or verdict. Parties must arrange training on the court’s electronic evidence presentation system with the deputy clerk before trial.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Initial scheduling conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Initial scheduling conference (trap): The senior lawyers ultimately responsible for the case must attend, and compliance with Local Rule 16.1(B), (C), and (D) is treated as “of the utmost importance”; noncompliance may draw sanctions under Local Rule 1.3. A continuance is given only if counsel is actually engaged on trial. Automatic disclosure under Local Rule 26.2(A) is due no later than 2 weeks after the conference, and no formal discovery may start until a party has fully complied with Local Rule 26.2. Plaintiff’s counsel must notify parties who have not answered or appeared of the conference date. All submissions must be e-filed unless leave is granted for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Junior lawyers
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Junior lawyers: A standing order (February 1, 2008) strongly encourages relatively inexperienced attorneys to handle court matters, including summary judgment arguments and trial examinations. They are held to full preparation standards, must have authority suited to the proceeding (for example, to agree to a discovery schedule), and must be supervised by a more experienced attorney at complex evidentiary hearings unless leave is granted.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Scheduling order and extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Scheduling order and extensions (trap): Summary judgment responses are due within 14 calendar days of the motion (per Local Rule 7.1), and all filings must conform to Local Rule 56.1. A joint status report (discovery, settlement, pending or contemplated motions, proposed pretrial and trial dates, other matters) is due 7 days before any further scheduling or status conference. Extensions are granted only for good cause supported by affidavits, other evidentiary materials, or record citations. The motion must give the reasons, summarize the discovery remaining, and give a date certain for completing it.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Civil jury trial: pretrial conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Civil jury trial: pretrial conference (trap): The pretrial conference is generally about 3 weeks before trial. Trial counsel must attend, and counsel must come authorized (or accompanied by someone authorized) to settle; “No excuses will be granted” from this. Pending motions are heard at the conference. A pretrial memorandum, preferably joint, is due 7 days before the conference, covering items (a) through (m), including stipulated facts (counsel must stipulate to all facts not genuinely disputed), witnesses and their purpose, expert qualifications, page-and-line deposition designations with objections, and damages. Extensions require exceptional cause; lateness may bring dismissal, default, or other sanctions. Filed separately at the same time: requests for instructions with authority, proposed special verdict forms or interrogatories, proposed voir

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Exhibit lists
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Exhibit lists: By the first day of trial and before empanelment, file exhibit lists in the Appendix A format: exhibits coming in without objection numbered in a single sequence regardless of proponent, and items subject to objection lettered in a single sequence. In non-jury cases plaintiff starts at 1 and defendant at 501, and objected items are lettered by party (“PL’s A,” “D’s A”).

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Non-jury civil trials (trap)
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Non-jury civil trials (trap): Direct testimony is by affidavit, in admissible form and numbered paragraphs; live direct needs a motion for good cause by 12 noon 2 weeks before trial. A witness must appear for cross only if written notice is given by 12 noon 2 weeks before trial. By 12 noon 6 weeks before trial the party with the burden serves (does not file) 3 copies of proposed findings and conclusions in numbered paragraphs. By 12 noon 4 weeks before trial the other side files a marked copy, underlining genuinely disputed findings and contested conclusions and bracketing findings whose admissibility is contested; unmarked findings come in as uncontested at the start of trial. Responses to any additional or substitute proposals are due 2 weeks before trial. By 12 noon 4 weeks before trial each party files witness lists with direct-testimony affidavit

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Criminal pretrial and pleas (trap)
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Criminal pretrial and pleas (trap): For the initial pretrial or status conference, a joint status report is due by noon the week before, covering proposed trial, suppression, or Rule 11 dates; pending or contemplated motions; likely resolution; interpreter needs; custody status; fugitive status; and other matters. The court will not accept a plea agreement waiving appeal rights without a reliable demonstration, after full hearing, that the waiver is knowing and voluntary. The written plea agreement and notice of whether detention may follow the plea go under seal to the courtroom deputy by 12:00 noon the day before the Rule 11 hearing.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Criminal jury trial
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Criminal jury trial: A further pretrial conference is held 1 week before trial; trial counsel must attend unless excused. 3 weeks before trial: the government discloses remaining Local Rule 116.2 exculpatory information and a general description of Rule 404(b) evidence; both sides produce witness statements (Jencks/Rule 26.2); and the parties file proposed voir dire, jury instructions, stipulated facts, motions in limine, and a trial brief. Replies on motions in limine are due 2 weeks later. The government gives witness names and addresses and premarked exhibits 1 week before trial; the defendant does the same 3 days before trial. Joint exhibit lists are filed by the first day of trial.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Paper courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Paper courtesy copies (trap): Submit a paper courtesy copy of every e-filed document relating to a dispositive motion, opposition, reply, or sur-reply, including all exhibits, stamped “Courtesy Copy: DO NOT SCAN” (standing order, June 28, 2006). “Dispositive motion” is defined broadly: motions to dismiss, for summary judgment, to suppress, for preliminary relief, for judgment as a matter of law, Daubert motions, and motions in limine. When a document is under seal, file a courtesy paper copy of the complete unredacted document filed in a contested matter.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Sealing (trap): Motions to seal memoranda and attachments in their entirety are generally denied; redact the public filing and seek to seal only truly confidential matter. Every motion to seal needs an affidavit explaining the need, or the docket clerk will not seal (standing order, May 15, 2015). Good cause must go beyond the parties’ agreement or a protective-order designation, and the attorney seeking protection is subject to Rule 11. If the designating party is not the filer, confer before filing where feasible. If there is a dispute or no meaningful chance to confer, file the full document under seal and file a redacted public version within 7 working days; otherwise the clerk will unseal it. Protective orders do not bind the court, which decides independently what goes into public opinions and pleadings.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Motions and hearings
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Motions and hearings: The judge likes reply and surreply briefs (20-page limit, per the survey’s reading of the Local Rules) but will strike “supplemental” replies. Post-argument, parties may bring new caselaw to the court’s attention. Motions to dismiss and for summary judgment are typically heard, with time limits as needed. Motion in limine page limits follow the Local Rules. Patent cases follow Local Rule 16.6. Video Markman tutorials are encouraged, are filed as part of the record, and require a courtesy copy 3 business days before the hearing.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Scheduling conference and discovery
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Scheduling conference and discovery: The judge schedules mediation at the initial scheduling conference, along with fact discovery, expert discovery, Daubert briefing, summary judgment briefing, and trial. Be ready to discuss the facts and legal issues, the discovery needed for effective settlement talks, proportionality, and any likely protective-order dispute; parties may propose bifurcated discovery to cut expenses. Status conferences are rare, held if counsel request one. Discovery motions are typically referred to the magistrate judge without a hearing; emergency discovery motions are considered rarely.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Daubert (trap)
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Daubert (trap): Daubert deadlines are set at the initial scheduling conference, and Daubert motions should not be filed as motions in limine just before trial. Move for a Daubert hearing well before the pretrial conference so a separate hearing can be scheduled.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Continuances and remote hearings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Continuances and remote hearings (trap): Do not assume a motion to continue will be granted; if the court has not ruled, contact the courtroom deputy. Last-minute continuance requests short of a true emergency are disfavored. Rule 16 conferences, status conferences, and non-complex dispositive motion hearings are typically held by Zoom. Criminal trials, pretrials, revocations, sentencings, and evidentiary hearings are in person; Zoom is considered on request for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Pretrial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Pretrial (trap): Trial briefs are required in civil and criminal cases (sometimes waived after extensive summary judgment briefing). In civil cases the joint pretrial memorandum and individual trial briefs are due 7 days before the final pretrial conference; other civil deadlines are set at the pretrial conference, and criminal deadlines in the pretrial order. Confer on deposition transcripts before trial; present unresolved objections early enough to give the court at least 3 business days to rule. Agreed exhibits are numbered and contested exhibits lettered, using the posted joint exhibit list templates. Provide courtesy copies of trial exhibits at trial in a binder. Any juror questionnaire (used in sensitive cases) should be short and submitted at the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Trial: Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. or 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., depending on trial length and the court’s schedule. Time limits vary by case. No podium requirement; chalks are encouraged where useful; rebuttal cases are generally allowed. Civil juries are 10; criminal trials have 2 to 4 alternates, empaneled separately. The judge puts voir dire to the whole venire, follows up at sidebar (counsel may ask follow-up questions), and peremptories go government first with no back challenging. Civil charge conferences are off the record; the jury gets a written charge. In bench trials submit proposed findings and conclusions before trial; supplements are typically allowed within 2 weeks after trial, and the court will not wait for a transcript.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: Criminal discovery is not handled by the judge. An initial pretrial conference is held at the close of discovery to complete the pretrial order and set a trial date; be ready to identify issues to resolve before trial (such as Daubert) and give a realistic witness count and trial length. Motions in limine on key evidentiary issues are preferred. The judge resolves release motions after referral back, holds hearings on detention review, and always holds a hearing on suppression motions. A sentencing memorandum is required when the guidelines are disputed or a variance or departure is sought. Expedited sentencing is allowed when the usual 90-day period would cause unnecessary incarceration, usually in illegal re-entry cases.

docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — Court-scheduled mediation
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. Court-scheduled mediation: The judge’s posted mediation order sets mediation at 10:00 a.m. by video conference. Counsel must attend with their clients or client representatives who have authority to negotiate and commit to settlement terms. All participants must take part in good faith and keep confidential all communications exchanged during the mediation.

docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — Confidential settlement memorandum (trap)
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. Confidential settlement memorandum (trap): No later than 5 days before the mediation, each party gives the court a confidential memorandum of no more than 5 pages covering: background and key issues, with a breakdown of claimed damages; the strongest and weakest legal and factual points of its own case; the same for the opposing party’s case; and the status of settlement talks, including each side’s last proposal. Counsel must confer and confirm the status of settlement proposals before submitting the memoranda.

docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — How to submit the memorandum
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. How to submit the memorandum: Email it to the courtroom deputy named in the order (the January 2023 form names Bethaney Healy, Bethaney_Healy@mad.uscourts.gov; the court’s September 2026 telephone directory lists a different courtroom deputy for Judge Ponsor, so check the order in your case). It is held in confidence, not docketed, not shared with the other side, and returned after the mediation.

docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — Objecting that the case is not ripe
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. Objecting that the case is not ripe: A party that believes the case is not ripe for mediation must notify opposing counsel and the court in writing within 3 workdays of receiving the order, briefly giving reasons. The other side may respond within 3 workdays after that; the court may or may not cancel or postpone.

docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — Rescheduling mediation (trap)
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. Rescheduling mediation (trap): Do not contact the deputy directly about rescheduling. Confer and, as soon as possible and no later than 1 week before the mediation, file an assented-to motion to continue offering at least 3 dates and times when all counsel and principals or representatives are available.

docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — Courtroom
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. Courtroom: Hampden Courtroom, U.S. Courthouse, 300 State Street, Springfield. Under the court-wide courtroom technology page, contact the courtroom deputy at least 2 weeks before trial to test equipment.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Scheduling conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Scheduling conference (trap): The Notice of Scheduling Conference stresses that the senior lawyers ultimately responsible for the case must attend and that compliance with L.R. 16.1(B), (C), and (D) (and L.R. 16.6 in patent cases) is “of the utmost importance.” Counsel may get a continuance only if actually engaged on trial, and noncompliance may draw sanctions under L.R. 1.3. Plaintiff’s counsel must notify any party or attorney who has not yet answered or appeared of the conference date. At the conference the judge usually sets only the fact-discovery schedule, makes a general inquiry about settlement and mediation, and does not generally ask about the likelihood of trial.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Case management: A further status conference is scheduled at the initial conference, to be held before the end of fact discovery. Topics depend on the case and may include discovery, whether the schedule still holds, mediation (especially the court-annexed ADR program), and pending problems. No added requirements on the L.R. 16.1(D)(3) budget and ADR certifications. Bifurcation of discovery is not the norm but may fit particular cases; proportionality is handled in a general assessment of discovery needs.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Discovery and protective orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Discovery and protective orders (trap): No typical practice on referral: the judge refers some discovery disputes to the magistrate judge and decides some, usually without a hearing. “Emergency” discovery disputes should be rare; most can be foreseen and resolved in the normal course. Any proposed protective order must provide that amendments to the order, once entered, must be approved by the court. No other format or timing requirement. Expert time limits in Fed. R. Civ. P. 26, Fed. R. Crim. P. 16, and L.R. 116.1 are strictly enforced. ESI is usually handled by a negotiated protocol.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Motions to dismiss and summary judgment motions are heard most of the time, generally with no time limits on argument. Replies and surreplies are typically allowed and have no page limit, but the judge expects them to be succinct and targeted. For motions with lengthy memoranda or supporting affidavits, the judge will often ask for courtesy paper copies. Post-argument briefs may be allowed, for example when a new issue arose at argument that the briefing did not adequately address.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Pro se cases
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Pro se cases: The judge may waive the L.R. 7.1 consultation obligation in cases with a pro se litigant.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Patent cases
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Patent cases: The judge generally follows the template in L.R. 16.6 (effective June 1, 2018) and has no particular Markman-hearing practice.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Criminal matters: Discovery issues ordinarily go to the magistrate judge during pretrial supervision, and the magistrate judge sets suppression-motion deadlines; suppression hearings are scheduled case by case. A motion for release or to modify release conditions filed after the case returns to the district judge is referred first to the magistrate judge. Motions for review of a detention order are typically heard.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Sentencing
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Sentencing: Sentencing memoranda are not required but are regarded as useful, to understand the parties’ positions before the hearing. The government must give advance notice that victim statements will be offered. Statements may be written or oral; oral statements are made from the podium.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Sealing (trap): Motions to seal memoranda and attachments in their entirety are generally denied. File a redacted version publicly as an attachment to a motion to file the unredacted document under seal, supported by an affidavit that identifies each redaction by page number and justifies each one with a particular factual showing of harm; conclusory statements will not do. The motion must comply with L.R. 7.2 and describe generally the material, the requested duration, and the legal grounds. Anyone may oppose within 7 days; if granted, within 7 days file the unredacted version under seal and the redacted version publicly, and serve the unredacted version on all parties. Party agreement or a discovery confidentiality order is not, by itself, a justification. When the party seeking protection is not the filer, confer before filing when feasible; if confer

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Protective orders
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Protective orders: No special format, but distinguish orders limiting use or disclosure during discovery from orders that purport to limit use of materials submitted to the court for substantive purposes. Counsel should review the sealing standing order.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Default judgment (trap)

For issues that might bottleneck discovery, parties have been invited to contact the courtroom deputy to arrange a brief telephone or Zoom hearing. With significant ESI, counsel should have a plan, especially where the parties’ capacities to handle ESI differ substantially.

docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Tailor the discovery discussion to the case; where potentially dispositive issues can be raised early at minimal cost, delaying or staggering discovery may make sense. A status conference often follows fact discovery, before large expert expenditures, covering mediation, schedule revisions, motions, and trial. Status conferences are commonly by Zoom.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Motions and discovery
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Motions and discovery: Motions to dismiss, summary judgment motions, and discovery motions are typically heard, with no time limits on argument. If issues are resolved or narrowed before the hearing, file a status report. Emergency discovery motions are heard when necessary, but the judge strongly encourages working issues out or agreeing to a stay.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Scheduling and case management
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Scheduling and case management: Separate scheduling orders apply to referral and consent cases. Both set a status conference before the end of fact discovery, preceded by a filed status report on expert discovery, dispositive motions, mediation interest, and other matters. In consent cases, motions to compel, for protective orders, to quash, and similar motions must be filed by the close of the relevant discovery period absent good cause; lead trial counsel must attend any pretrial conference; and the L.R. 16.5(D) pretrial memorandum is due 5 business days before the initial pretrial conference.

Due the same day: agreed jury instructions (alternatives with authority if no agreement; none needed on preliminary matters), motions in limine, and, for jury cases, a trial brief with a neutral statement of the case for the

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Trial: Courtroom 14, 5th floor. Expect a full first day, then 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. until the case goes to the jury; bench trials may run full days. Chalks are fine if shown to opposing counsel in advance without meritorious objection. A draft jury charge is docketed and discussed with counsel, and jurors get a written copy and may use notebooks. Avoid eliciting personal data (Social Security and account numbers, minors’ names, birth dates, home addresses) in testimony.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Inexperienced attorneys
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Inexperienced attorneys: The judge strongly encourages relatively inexperienced attorneys, and the attorney who wrote most of the papers, to appear at conferences, hearings, and trials. They must be fully prepared and suitably authorized, and need supervision by a more experienced attorney for complex evidentiary work unless the court allows otherwise.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Remote appearances and criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Remote appearances and criminal matters: Civil and criminal status conferences are routinely by Zoom; other Zoom requests are considered case by case. A criminal case is referred back to the district judge when discovery is substantially complete. A defendant’s waiver of appearance at arraignment form is posted.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Motions and briefing
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Motions and briefing: Replies and sur-replies only on motion, and only when needed to address specific points in the response; no separate page limit is set. Post-argument briefs only to address a previously undiscussed issue raised at the hearing.

docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Scheduling and case management: No additional Local Rule 16.1(D) topics. Discovery may be bifurcated when there is a Monell claim. A case management or status conference is held at or near the close of fact discovery (discovery status, mediation, trial schedule); the trial date is set then. Parties may request telephonic conferences. Motions to extend scheduling-order deadlines need good cause and must state the reasons, the discovery remaining, and a specific completion date.

docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Pretrial: No initial pretrial conference is typically held in civil cases, though the form order provides for one: the pretrial memorandum under Local Rule 16.5(D) is due 5 business days before, omitting matters under Local Rule 16.5(D)(2) or (3). Proposed voir dire, jury instructions, verdict forms, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine are typically due 1 week before the pretrial conference, in no particular format. docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Trial: Trial runs Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. The judge seats 8 jurors in civil trials. Courtroom 1, Worcester.

Confer with clients beforehand; exchanging proposals in advance is encouraged. A party with decision-making authority must be present; request any deviation well in advance. Counsel attend with clients or representatives with unlimited authority. Typically no opening statements; separate caucuses, kept confidential unless authorized.

docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Status conferences may be attended by phone, and are canceled if the parties file a joint memo addressing the Local Rule and agree on excluding time.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Pro se cases and newer lawyers
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Standing order (May 6, 2019) strongly encourages relatively inexperienced attorneys, and the attorney who wrote most of the papers, to argue and examine witnesses. All attorneys must be fully prepared and carry authority suited to the proceeding (for example, to agree to a discovery schedule at a scheduling conference); inexperienced attorneys examining witnesses in complex evidentiary hearings or at trial must be supervised by a more experienced attorney unless the court grants leave.

docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Remote proceedings: The judge routinely conducts civil status conferences and motion hearings by Zoom; criminal defendants choose whether to appear by Zoom. docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Trial: Evidence days run 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.; 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. once deliberations begin. 8–9 jurors in civil trials. Courtroom 23, 7th floor, Boston. Rebuttal cases need a reasoned justification; in bench trials no traditional jury-style opening is expected.

Avoid eliciting Rule 5.2 personal data in testimony, since it becomes public in the transcript.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Pretrial and trial
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Pretrial and trial: A trial brief is required, per the order setting the case for trial. Pretrial deadlines and motion in limine page limits are set case by case; some motions in limine are resolved at the initial pretrial conference. Courtesy copies of trial exhibits, in a binder and on a flash drive, are typically due several weeks before trial. Number every exhibit uniquely (no plaintiff’s or defendant’s exhibits; decimals for groups, such as 5.1); numbers never change even if an exhibit is excluded. Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.; 8 civil jurors. Share chalks with opposing counsel before the day they are used. Rebuttal only for issues counsel could not reasonably have anticipated. The judge circulates a draft charge and verdict form before the charge conference; jurors get a written charge. Proposed findings may be filed in bench trials.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: Parties are reminded to confer and timely file the joint status memorandum due 7 days before a status conference. Cases return to the district judge when discovery is complete.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Scheduling and status conferences
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Scheduling and status conferences: No scheduling order or topics beyond Local Rule 16.1(D), and no added budget or ADR conferral requirements. At the initial conference the judge asks whether the parties have discussed settlement and encourages early mediation. The initial schedule typically runs through discovery to the filing of dispositive motions, including plaintiff’s and defendant’s expert disclosure deadlines; Daubert schedules are set at the parties’ request. A mid-discovery status conference is typically set to check that discovery is on track and to surface emerging disputes.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Discovery: In large-scale e-discovery cases, the parties are expected to arrive with a plan covering production formats, timelines, and, if applicable, search terms. Counsel should have discussed proportionality before the conference. No protective-order deadline, but the judge prefers that parties first try to negotiate a confidentiality agreement before seeking a protective order. Discovery motions are typically heard; the judge may use the hearing as an informal discussion to reach a resolution without a formal order, but expects the parties to have already worked to resolve the issue. Emergency discovery motions are most likely considered when an imminent event is at stake and the dispute could not have been foreseen.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions and replies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions and replies (trap): Replies and surreplies are typically allowed if there is reason to think they will help, but they must not restate prior briefing. No set page limit, but a motion for leave must state specifically how many pages are sought. Motions to dismiss are typically heard (straightforward legal issues may be decided on the papers); summary judgment motions are heard. No usual time limits on argument. Post-argument briefing only if the court requests it. Paper courtesy copies are not required as a matter of course but may be requested for particularly voluminous submissions.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Mediation (trap)
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Mediation (trap): Each party must submit a confidential memorandum of up to five pages on the issues expected at mediation. The judge has no standard pre-mediation order. After introductions, the parties typically move to individual sessions. A party wanting opening statements first must request it in its memorandum and briefly explain why they would help. The judge prefers that a party with decision-making authority be present, but may allow participation by phone depending on the circumstances.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: No practices beyond Local Rule 116.5 for status conferences and none for scheduling. Cases typically go back to the district judge when discovery is complete.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Pretrial
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Pretrial: A trial brief is required. The trial date is set at the status conference after the close of discovery. At the initial pretrial conference, be ready to discuss anticipated legal and evidentiary issues, stipulations, number of witnesses, and estimated trial length. Voir dire, jury instructions, verdict forms, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine are typically due before the final pretrial conference; any required format will be set in the pretrial procedural order. Motions in limine (no page limit) and Daubert motions are typically heard and resolved at the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Trial exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Trial exhibits (trap): Courtesy copies of trial exhibits are required: before the final pretrial conference if there are exhibit disputes, otherwise at the outset of trial, in a form that depends on the case. Exhibits must be pre-marked; discuss the marking method with the courtroom deputy before trial.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Trial schedule and practice
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Trial schedule and practice: Full trial days, 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., with a 15–30 minute morning break, an hour-long lunch, and a 15–30 minute afternoon break. Request a different schedule in the joint pretrial memorandum. Expect time limits on openings and closings; state how long you need in the joint pretrial memorandum. No time limits on presenting evidence. Use of the podium is not required. Four rounds of examination (direct, cross, redirect, recross); a rebuttal case is allowed if the party shows why it is appropriate. Chalks may be used, but show any opening chalk to opposing counsel first. The jury receives a written copy of the charge.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Scheduling and status conferences
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Scheduling and status conferences: No scheduling order or topics beyond Local Rule 16.1(D). At the initial conference the judge asks about mediation and the likelihood of dispositive motions and trial, and sets the schedule for all discovery, dispositive motions, Daubert motions, and any Markman hearing; expert and Daubert deadlines may later be modified. Be ready to address the number and identity of deponents, and for ESI, where the information is located and the plan for retrieval and preservation. Status conferences are held every 60 to 90 days on the status of discovery and the ability to meet the original schedule.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Discovery motions
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Discovery motions: No requirements beyond Local Rule 37.1(A) conferral. Discovery motions are typically heard and usually ruled on orally from the bench. Emergency discovery motions are generally considered, depending on the circumstances. Bifurcation of discovery is rare, with cost a major factor.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Replies and surreplies are typically allowed, with a page limit. Motions to dismiss and summary judgment motions are typically heard; argument time varies. Post-argument briefs are rare. Paper courtesy copies are required only on rare occasions when documents are voluminous.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Mediation (trap)
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Mediation (trap): Counsel and parties must attend with full settlement authority; a party’s presence is excused only by court order. A brief mediation memorandum addressing the merits and the party’s settlement position is due three business days before the hearing, marked “Confidential - Not for docketing,” and is not served on the other side (the 2017 sample notice directs submission by fax or email to the courtroom deputy). If the case is not ripe for mediation, contact the courtroom deputy. If the date poses a serious conflict, do not call the deputy: confer and file an assented-to motion to continue proposing several dates when all counsel and principals are available.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Pretrial memorandum (trap)
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Pretrial memorandum (trap): The sample orders require a pretrial memorandum (joint or separate) about one week before the final pretrial conference, covering: a summary of each side’s evidence on liability and damages; established facts; contested facts; jurisdictional questions; pending-motion issues; issues of law, including evidentiary questions, with authority; requested pleading amendments; other matters; probable trial length; witnesses with addresses and the purpose of each one’s testimony (with a brief statement of qualifications for any expert whose qualifications are not admitted); proposed exhibits; and whether daily transcript copy is needed. Written notice of objections to an expert’s qualifications or to any proposed exhibit, with supporting authority, is due to all parties by the same date and must be filed with the Clerk. Noncompliance

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Jury trial additions
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Jury trial additions: In jury cases, the memorandum must also include proposed questions for the venire and joint proposed jury instructions. Where the parties cannot agree, alternative instructions must cite legal authority for the specific language; none are needed on preliminary matters such as burden of proof and credibility. Instructions may be submitted during trial only if the evidence develops otherwise than reasonably anticipated; otherwise leave of court is required. Notify the court immediately if the case will not go to trial, and disregard the jury instructions if the parties elect a jury-waived trial.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Motions in limine and Daubert
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Motions in limine and Daubert: No page limit for motions in limine. They are heard sometimes at the final pretrial conference and sometimes on the first day of trial. Daubert motions are resolved earlier in the case. A juror questionnaire is a case-specific decision; propose it, as the proposed questions, at the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Trial (trap): Trial days run 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. The trial date is set after discovery closes and dispositive motions are resolved. No preset time limits, but the judge asks counsel’s estimates and may limit time that seems excessive. Courtesy copies of trial exhibits, in a binder, are due on the first day of trial. Pre-mark stipulated exhibits: plaintiff by numbers, defendant by letters. Counsel must use the podium. Examination goes through recross. Chalks during openings and closings must be by agreement. The jury receives a written copy of the charge; special verdict forms should be in final format.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Jury selection: No attorney voir dire. The panel is sworn, questions are asked and responses heard at sidebar; once the panel is declared indifferent the clerk fills the box, counsel get a few minutes, challenges are heard at sidebar, and removed jurors are replaced.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: No practices beyond Local Rule 116.5. Cases go back to the district judge when the defendant indicates a trial or plea or there is a dispositive motion schedule.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — Recall status and role
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Recall status and role: Judge Neiman, a recalled magistrate judge in Springfield (Hampden Courtroom), concentrates on mediation. The judge posts practices only for mediation.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — Attendance and format (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Attendance and format (trap): The posted mediation order schedules the conference by video conference. Counsel must be present with their clients or client representatives who have no limitation on authority to negotiate and commit to settlement terms. The judge requires a party with decision-making authority to be present, though on occasion someone may be allowed to participate by telephone.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — Confidential settlement memorandum (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Confidential settlement memorandum (trap): Each party submits, under seal and to the judge alone, an updated confidential settlement memorandum of no more than four pages, by the date set in the order (the survey says about five days before the mediation). Email it to Tamara_Figueroa@Mad.uscourts.gov. It must candidly address: the key issues, with a specific breakdown of claimed damages; the strongest and weakest legal and factual points in the party’s own case and in the opponent’s; the status of negotiations, including each side’s last proposal; the settlement the party believes would be fair; and the proposal the party would make to conclude the matter now. Memoranda are held in confidence and returned at the end of mediation.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — Before the mediation
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Before the mediation: Counsel must confer with their clients in advance to explore settlement positions, and the parties are encouraged to exchange settlement proposals before the conference. If a party believes the case is not ripe for mediation, notify other counsel and the court as soon as possible.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — Confidentiality terms
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Confidentiality terms: By participating, all parties, counsel, and participants agree to mediate in good faith; that the entire process, including any in-person, video, or audio part, is confidential; that statements are privileged settlement discussions, without prejudice and inadmissible for any purpose; and that no one will seek to compel the mediator to testify or produce documents.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — How the mediation runs
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. How the mediation runs: The judge meets jointly with the parties and counsel first, asks each side’s understanding of the last demand and offer, and does not want to hear bottom or top lines. When appropriate, the judge then shuttles between the parties exchanging offers and demands.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — Consent to magistrate judge jurisdiction (Western Division, 2012)
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Consent to magistrate judge jurisdiction (Western Division, 2012): Under the February 13, 2012 Western Division standing order, three of eight civil cases (excluding bankruptcy appeals, § 2255 cases, and cases seeking an immediate TRO) were randomly assigned to Judge Neiman. Filing the consent-or-refusal form is mandatory within 30 days of service on the last party, though consent itself is voluntary; plaintiff (or the removing party) serves the order and form and files one form for the case, without identifying any party that refuses. Pro se prisoner cases: each party files its own consent or refusal on paper marked “DO NOT SCAN.” Given the judge’s recall status, check whether this assignment system still applies to your case.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Discovery motions
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Discovery motions: No requirements beyond Local Rule 37.1(A) conferral, but the judge works with counsel on the most efficient way to present a discovery issue: full memoranda, letters, a telephone conference, or an informal conference. The judge generally holds fairly significant hearings on discovery motions, rules from the bench when possible, and usually issues the order (occasionally asking the parties to draft it). Less experienced attorneys are encouraged to argue, particularly associates who know the facts. Emergency discovery motions are considered only for a real emergency; the judge rarely decides a motion without giving the opposing party a substantive chance to respond.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Summary judgment and dispositive motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Summary judgment and dispositive motions (trap): For summary judgment, the judge requests one document stating the undisputed facts together with the opposing party’s response to each. Replies are generally allowed but must be very short and focused; surreplies are not encouraged. No courtesy copies of exhibits or depositions unless the court requests them. Motions to dismiss and summary judgment motions are typically heard, with no time limits on argument. The judge may request more briefing, and new cases can be brought to the court’s attention by post-argument brief.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Mediation (trap)
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Mediation (trap): An electronic order in each case requires counsel to attend with clients or representatives with full settlement authority; a decision maker may be available by phone only occasionally and with prior permission. No later than 3 business days before the conference, each party submits (by mail, hand delivery, or email as the order directs) a brief memorandum marked “Confidential - Not for Docketing” on the merits and settlement. Bring any standard form settlement agreement you use, and tell opposing counsel and the court as soon as possible if the case is not ripe for mediation. No opening statements. The judge meets each counsel alone beforehand (without clients), meets everyone to review the rules, then separates the parties for shuttle diplomacy.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Scheduling and status conferences
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Scheduling and status conferences: The judge follows Local Rule 16.1(D) with no separate scheduling order or added joint-statement topics. At the initial conference the judge always asks about mediation, usually sets fact and expert discovery, and often defers dispositive-motion deadlines to the next status conference. Be ready to discuss the substance of the case, potential discovery and ESI problems, and the best form for presenting discovery disputes. Proportionality is left for the parties to raise; protective orders need no particular format or timing. The first status conference is usually near the close of fact discovery and covers discovery status, schedule changes, mediation, and whether dispositive motions are likely (often scheduled when fact discovery is almost complete).

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Pretrial
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Pretrial: Trial briefs and an initial pretrial conference follow the Local Rules. Deadlines for voir dire, jury instructions, verdict forms, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine are set with the trial date, usually 1–2 weeks before trial. No special format or courtesy copy for voir dire, instructions, or verdict forms unless requested. No page limit for motions in limine; they are heard at the final pretrial conference unless other arrangements are made, and resolved as early as possible. Daubert motions are scheduled closer to trial, but the judge prefers to address them as early as possible.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Trial exhibits
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Trial exhibits: Courtesy copies of trial exhibits are required: disputed exhibits are filed with the appropriate motion; others can be provided at trial. The judge prefers at least one hard copy. Exhibits must be pre-marked, with the parties trying to agree on a numbering scheme. Under the court’s general courtroom-technology page, contact the courtroom deputy at least two weeks before trial to test equipment.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Trial: Civil trial dates are set at the close of discovery or after summary judgment and can usually be scheduled within a few months. Shorter trials run 10 to 4; longer trials 9:30 to 1:00. No time limits on openings, evidence, or closings. The judge asks all voir dire questions of the venire, then questions individually at sidebar anyone who answered yes, with counsel’s input. Nine jurors are seated in civil trials. Attorney voir dire and juror questionnaires have not been used but will be considered if counsel ask. No podium requirement; direct, cross, redirect, and recross are allowed. Chalks in openings and closings must be pre-approved by opposing counsel. The charge is reviewed item by item with counsel, a written copy goes to the jury on request after consultation, and proposed special verdict forms are welcome in any format.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Bench trials
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Bench trials: The judge appreciates an opening and a closing; closings are sometimes deferred until after proposed findings and rulings are submitted, and detailed proposed findings may not be required before trial, depending on its length.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Criminal and pro se matters
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Criminal and pro se matters: Criminal status conferences are usually held within 1 month, with exceptions; the case returns to the district judge when discovery is complete or will be completed without further magistrate involvement. With pro se litigants, the judge makes sure the litigant understands the process and discusses appointing pro bono counsel for mediation only.

Lead trial counsel must appear at all conferences and hearings, including scheduling conferences. No special appearances. docs.x: Judge David O. Carter, C.D. Cal.. docs.t: Judge David O. Carter (C.D. Cal.) — Ex parte applications
docs.x: Judge David O. Carter, C.D. Cal.. Ex parte applications: Decided on the papers and usually not set for hearing. docs.x: Judge David O. Carter, C.D. Cal.. Continuances and calendar conflicts (trap): Changes are disfavored and need good cause with a detailed, compelling factual explanation. For a calendar conflict, seek a stipulation from all opposing counsel to move the hearing; failing that, file an ex parte application well before the hearing.

docs.t: Judge David O. Carter (C.D. Cal.) — Sealing

docs.t: Judge Fernando Aenlle-Rocha (C.D. Cal.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Fernando Aenlle-Rocha, C.D. Cal.. Trial: Trials start Mondays and run Monday to Thursday, 8:15 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.; Fridays are reserved for the calendar, but deliberations run Monday to Friday. Civil juries are generally eight; the court conducts voir dire with a written questionnaire, and each side gets three peremptory challenges. On day one, give the courtroom deputy three sets of tabbed exhibit binders (one original for the jury, two copies), a USB drive of all exhibits, and any deposition excerpts. Exhibits are numbered 1, 2, 3 (not 1.1), with yellow (plaintiff) and blue (defendant) tags. Meet and confer at least 10 days before trial on foundation and exhibits to be received. Request RealTime or daily transcripts at least 14 days ahead. No speaking objections; one lawyer per witness. In bench trials, no post-trial briefs unless authorized.

Patent: the Patent Standing Order is incorporated, and contentions cannot be amended without a timely showing of good cause.

Oral argument on dispositive motions is not routine but may be requested. Discovery goes to the magistrate judge. She conducts her own pretrial conferences. Almost all cases go to mediation; she doesn’t hold settlement conferences but may refer one to a magistrate judge.

docs.t: Judge Susan C. Bucklew (M.D. Fla.) — Criminal
docs.x: Judge Susan C. Bucklew, M.D. Fla.. Criminal: Pleas and discovery usually go to the magistrate judge. Sentencings 8:30 to 9:30 a.m., Tuesday through Friday; tell the courtroom deputy if one will exceed 30 minutes.

docs.t: Judge Susan C. Bucklew (M.D. Fla.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Susan C. Bucklew, M.D. Fla.. Trial: Trial calendar the month before the term; criminal cases first; dates certain only in exceptional cases. Jury instructions, verdict forms, and voir dire five days before jury selection, with copies emailed to chambers. Lawyers usually get a short voir dire. E-file exhibit and witness lists by the morning of trial and email copies in WordPerfect; bring a three-ring binder of premarked exhibits for the court.

docs.t: Judge Henry Lee Adams Jr. (M.D. Fla.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Henry Lee Adams Jr., M.D. Fla.. Motions: Dispositive motions need pinpoint citations. Deposition excerpts are accepted for summary judgment, but he may later ask for full transcripts. The motions-in-limine deadline is set at the pretrial conference. Don’t docket proposed orders with the motion; follow the Administrative Procedures.

docs.x: Judge Mark C. Scarsi, C.D. Cal.. Criminal cases: The government must produce discovery in its possession, including Brady material, within 7 days of the post-indictment arraignment; a joint discovery report is due within 14 days. Trial evidence produced later than 2 weeks before trial is excluded unless the court approves an ex parte application. Motions are filed 14 days before the hearing (10 pages); oppositions 7 days before (10 pages); optional replies by noon 3 days before (5 pages). Motions in limine are heard at the FPTC. Continuance requests are due at least 7 calendar days before the date. Sentencing is set at least 14 weeks after the plea; sentencing briefs are due 14 days before. Sentencing videos are discouraged, limited to 10 minutes, and need a transcript. For open pleas, file a factual-basis stipulation 7 days before the hearing. docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Hearings and tentative rulings
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Hearings and tentative rulings: Civil motions Mondays at 1:30 p.m.; criminal motions Mondays at 9 a.m. (if Monday is a holiday, the following Monday). No need to clear a date first. Discovery motions go to the magistrate judge. Courtroom 10C, Santa Ana. The court tries to issue tentatives on each motion, generally posted by mid-afternoon on the Friday before a Monday hearing (the page also says after noon on the business day before and about a half hour before the hearing in the courtroom). Read it in advance and focus argument; if all parties submit on it, tell the deputy and no appearance is needed. If oral argument won’t help, the court says so by the Friday before the hearing.

No special appearances: counsel of record must appear. Lead counsel must appear at dispositive motions, scheduling conferences, and settlement conferences, and all attorneys must attend pretrial conferences in person.

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Briefs and motions (trap)

A Rule 12 motion must attach the challenged pleading. Motions to amend must attach a redline of the amended pleading, and an amended pleading filed after dismissal with leave must attach a redline appendix. If a motion or set of concurrently noticed motions involves more than 3 pleadings, the mover files an index with docket numbers within 3 days of filing and an updated index within 3 days of the reply. Any order seeking dates must state every proposed date; a reference to a stipulation is not enough.

Applications and stipulations to extend must state the existing date, concrete good cause (“will promote settlement” alone is insufficient; describe negotiation status), and prior requests. Stipulations need a proposed order with the dates and have no effect until approved. Proposed judgments endorsed by the other side are entered immediately; others are held 7 days for objections.
