docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Removal and fictitious defendants
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Removal and fictitious defendants: Removing defendants must refile all state court papers and serve the Initial Order on all parties; pending state motions must be re-noticed under L.R. 7. In diversity removals, identify and serve Doe defendants within 120 days; extensions and substitutions are sought by ex parte application, with 7 days for others to respond, addressing whether remand would follow if diversity is destroyed.

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Scheduling conference: Joint Rule 26(f) Report due at least 1 week before the conference, drafted by plaintiff as a single report covering items (a) through (n), including damages range, insurance, number of depositions, settlement mechanism, and trial estimate (be ready to explain over 8 court days). Exhibit A (presumptive schedule) is mandatory: proposed dates must be Mondays, trial a Tuesday. The court may decide the schedule on the papers; begin discovery early, as tight deadlines will be set. Lead trial counsel must attend. ERISA cases must address standard of review and preemption; patent cases must propose claim construction dates (N.D. Cal. patent rules); RICO plaintiffs must file a detailed RICO case statement within 20 days of that order.

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Discovery deadlines (trap)
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Discovery deadlines (trap): Depositions must start at least 5 working days before the cut-off; interrogatories, document requests, and requests for admission must be served at least 45 days before. Stipulations allowing responses after the cut-off are approved only in extraordinary circumstances. Motions on inadequate responses must be filed within 10 days after the cut-off. Repeated resort to the court on discovery may lead to a special master at the parties’ joint expense. Amendments and joinder must be filed within 60 days of the trial order and heard within 90.

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Motions in limine (trap): Filed at least 4 weeks before the pretrial conference, oppositions 3 weeks, replies 2 weeks; heard at the pretrial conference. Limit of 4 per side, not counting Rule 37(c)(1) and Daubert motions (state the basis in the caption title); more require an ex parte application 7 days before the due date. Deemed made and granted: exclusion of Rule 408 settlement evidence without an offer of proof outside the jury’s presence, and of undisclosed expert opinions.

docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Voir dire questions at least 4 court days before trial; one-page joint statement of the case 5 days before. The page says plaintiff submits the verdict form before the close of its case in chief (the 2013 order says the first day of trial). Questionnaires are discouraged and due 30 days before trial. Trial starts at 8:30 a.m. on day one; short trials (under 10 days) run 9 a.m. to noon and 1:30 to 4:30 p.m., longer ones 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. with no lunch. Meet 10 days before trial to s

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Court trial and criminal cases
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Court trial and criminal cases: Court trials: all direct testimony is by declaration, filed by the claimant’s side 20 days before trial and the defending side 13 days before; objections 5 days before trial. Witnesses then authenticate and are cross-examined. Criminal: memoranda capped at 25 pages, replies 12; Times Roman at least 14 point or Courier 12; no supplemental briefs without leave. Discovery motions require prior consultation and particulars or won’t be heard. Change of plea within 30 days of a fully executed plea agreement; government lodges witness statements in camera 5 calendar days before trial; instructions due 1 week before trial; voir dire 5 court days before. A draft sentencing memorandum is generally available 15 minutes before sentencing.

Motions to amend must state the effect of the amendment and identify the page, line, and wording of each change, with a Notice of Lodging of the proposed pleading and a redline appendix. Deliver the redline to opposing counsel at least two hours before the L.R. 7-3 conference; if the draft changes, confer again. Default judgment motions are due within 14 days after default against the last defendant or resolution of all other claims, must show subject-matter and personal jurisdiction, and must include any fee and cost request (a later fee motion will be stricken absent good cause). docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Ex parte applications and TROs: Only for extraordinary relief, with a showing of irreparable prejudice and that the movant is without fault or acted with excusable neglect (Mission Power). Decided on the papers; don’t set a hearing. Any opposition or notice of non-opposition is due 24 hours after receipt of the application or 24 hours after it is filed, whichever is earlier. The same deadline applies to TRO oppositions, and the court won’t rule on a TRO until at least 24 hours after service unless notice is excused or justice requires.

docs.t: Judge Fred W. Slaughter (C.D. Cal.) — Continuances and stipulations
docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Continuances and stipulations: Good cause only, judged by diligence and prejudice. Requests must be by stipulation, motion, or application with a declaration giving the reasons and any prior continuance requests and their outcome. Stipulations aren’t effective until approved, and every stipulation or request to alter time must propose new dates for all affected deadlines. Criminal cases: confer on new dates and email the courtroom deputy to confirm availability before filing any continuance request. Calendar conflicts: notify both judges’ courtroom deputies at least 3 days ahead and defer to the more senior judge. A “Notice of Unavailability” has no effect and should not be filed.

docs.t: Judge Fred W. Slaughter (C.D. Cal.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Sealing: Civil: follow L.R. 79-5. Justify each item under the good cause or compelling reasons standard; blanket claims or meritless requests will be denied. Meet and confer before filing an application to seal, and file a redacted public version where redaction is feasible. Criminal: e-file the application with a proposed order that includes an alternative line in case of denial, then email PDFs and a Word proposed order to FWS_Chambers@cacd.uscourts.gov with the case number and “UNDER SEAL REQUEST” in the subject. Bracket and highlight redacted portions in the unredacted copies. Use a generic cover sheet title if the real title is confidential. Non-paper exhibits go to the Clerk’s intake on USB, not CD.

Meet and confer and specific motions: Failure to meet and confer under L.R. 7-3 risks summary denial, and a nonmoving party that ignores timely efforts to confer risks sanctions. docs.t: Judge Josephine Staton (C.D. Cal.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josephine Staton, C.D. Cal.. Summary judgment (trap): Each party may file only one summary judgment motion in the case, though it need not wait for the motion cutoff. Use tabs, tables of contents, and indices to make the papers easy to absorb. The Statement of Genuine Disputes must track the movant’s statement exactly in two columns, with the movant’s fact and evidence combined in the left column and “undisputed” or “disputed” (with reasons, evidence cites, and a description of what in the evidence refutes the fact) in the right. docs.t: Judge Josephine Staton (C.D. Cal.) — Ex parte applications
docs.x: Judge Josephine Staton, C.D. Cal.. Ex parte applications: Extraordinary relief only, and the applicant must show the need is not due to its own lack of diligence. Determine the other side’s position beforehand and state it in the application or a declaration. Tell the opponent any opposition is due within 24 hours after service. No replies without leave. If you will not oppose, email the courtroom deputy as soon as possible. Applications are usually decided on the papers and almost never granted without giving the other side a chance to respond.

Stipulations are ineffective until approved, and the court generally will not rule on “rush” stipulations to relieve parties of filing deadlines.

Explain any deviation. Choose ADR Procedure No. 2 (Court Mediation Panel) or No. 3 (private mediation); No. 1 (magistrate judge) is not available to elect. Put a hearing time estimate on the caption of motions and oppositions. docs.x: Judge Josephine Staton, C.D. Cal.. Settlement, fees, and judgments: On settlement of all claims, the court stays the case and expects a stipulation of dismissal within 30 days; no stay for tentative settlements or settlements in principle. The court generally won’t retain jurisdiction to enforce unless the agreement is filed under seal for review. Fee motions (other than L.R. 55-3 schedule fees) need an Excel spreadsheet listing each task on its own line: date, timekeeper, description, hourly rate, time, and a formula calculating the fee. E-file it as a PDF exhibit and email the Excel file to chambers. No Rule 54(b) partial judgment without a granted motion. When all claims are resolved, the prevailing party lodges and emails a Rule 58(a) proposed judgment.

Settlement: The scheduling order sets an attorney settlement conference deadline: a good-faith counsel discussion of settlement and mediation, not a court conference. Parties who can afford private mediation should use it before asking for a settlement judge; others may request a pro bono mediator under LCR 39.1(c)(4). After failed mediation, request a magistrate judge settlement conference by email to the deputy.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany M. Cartwright (W.D. Wash.) — Trial days
docs.x: Judge Tiffany M. Cartwright, W.D. Wash.. Trial days: Trial runs Monday through Friday (Tuesdays may be shortened for criminal in-custody hearings, with advance notice). Courtroom opens about 8:15 a.m.; pretrial matters at 8:30 or 8:45 a.m.; 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. with lunch 12:00 to 1:30 p.m. (issues outside the jury’s presence at 1:15 p.m.). Voir dire begins at 9:00 a.m. on day one; each side usually gets 20 minutes after the court’s questions. Be ready for openings and the first witness that afternoon. Have enough witnesses to fill each day; the judge will not recess early or delay trial for an unavailable witness.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany M. Cartwright (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tiffany M. Cartwright, W.D. Wash.. Trial exhibits (trap): Each party brings two tabbed binders of paper exhibits (sides marked “Clerk” and “Judge”) and two thumb drives to the courtroom deputy the morning of trial, unless the deputy instructs otherwise. The jury reviews admitted exhibits electronically. Pre-mark every exhibit with cause number, party and exhibit number, and a blank “Admitted” line. Plaintiff numbers 001 to 499; defendant from 500. List each document once; any party may use a listed exhibit. Electronic exhibits as searchable (OCR) PDFs named like the paper ones; audio or video must play in Windows Media Player or VLC. Email a joint exhibit list in Word (auto-numbering off) to the deputy before trial; exhibits newly admitted during trial are reported daily with PDFs or a thumb drive and new paper copies. Get trained on the courtroom technology before day one.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany M. Cartwright (W.D. Wash.) — Jury instructions and designations
docs.x: Judge Tiffany M. Cartwright, W.D. Wash.. Jury instructions and designations: The jury is instructed twice: before openings and after the evidence. The judge’s standard set (Ninth Circuit Model Civil 1.3, 1.5, 1.6 or 1.7, 1.8 when applicable, 1.9 through 1.18, 1.20, and 1.21 at the start; 2.16, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, and 3.5 at the end) need not be submitted; raise objections to it at the pretrial conference. Submit agreed instructions plus each side’s disputed ones with explanations and citations, in LCR 51 format, with a proposed verdict form; file on ECF and email Word to cartwrightorders@wawd.uscourts.gov. Besides LCR 32(e) highlighting, provide a separate chart for each deposition listing page and line, the opposing party’s objection, and the offering party’s response.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — No noting dates (trap)
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. No noting dates (trap): Judge Rothstein does not use the Local Rules’ noting dates. For ALL motions, oppositions are due 21 days after the motion is filed and replies 14 days after the opposition; these dates control over the Local Rules.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Briefs and page limits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Briefs and page limits (trap): Motion and argument in a single document, with no table of cases or table of authorities. Motions, oppositions, and objections: 15 pages; replies: 10 pages (excluding certificate of service). Sur-replies need leave; overlength motions are granted only for extraordinary complexity. Double-spaced, 12-point Times New Roman (footnotes too, but they may be single-spaced), page numbers, margins of at least 1 inch. Noncompliant filings may be summarily denied or stricken. Email a Word proposed order with every motion and stipulation to rothsteinorders@wawd.uscourts.gov.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Meet and confer (trap)
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Meet and confer (trap): Every non-dispositive motion needs a conferral certification, placed visibly in the first substantive paragraph or the final paragraph. Allow at least three business days between attempts to confer and filing, and explain specific efforts if contact failed. Rule 12(b) motions also require prior conferral and certification, to see whether amendment can avoid the motion; parties should try not to oppose timely motions to amend.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Summary judgment: MSJ and opposition: 24 pages; reply: 12 pages; sur-reply only with leave. May be filed any time before the dispositive motion deadline. Two-party cross-motions: counsel agree who moves first; the other side files one combined cross-motion/opposition, then opposition/reply, then reply. In multi-party cases with more than two movants, submit a proposed briefing schedule before filing.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Discovery disputes (trap): No opposed discovery motion until the parties meaningfully confer under FRCP 37(a)(1) and then hold a telephone or video conference with the court. To arrange it, all counsel (not staff) send a joint email to Rothstein_Chambers@dcd.uscourts.gov with a one-paragraph joint description and three available dates and time ranges, stating Eastern or Pacific Time. Raise disputes in time to finish within the discovery deadline, or the challenge may be waived. A permitted motion must quote or attach the request and objection verbatim; the losing party may be sanctioned. Give third parties notice of these procedures; if discovery is referred to a magistrate judge, contact that judge first.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Extensions and rescheduling
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Extensions and rescheduling: Extensions are discouraged and need evident good cause, even if unopposed; press of other business ordinarily isn’t enough. File at least three business days before the deadline; oppositions within two business days. Motions to reschedule a hearing: at least five business days before it, with alternative dates available to all parties, or the court picks a date.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Hearings and courtroom
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Hearings and courtroom: The court may decide any motion on the briefs and will contact the parties if it wants argument: 20 minutes per side plus 5 minutes rebuttal unless ordered otherwise. Counsel with authority to make all decisions must attend every appearance. Rise to address the court and stay at the podium unless permitted to approach.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Courtesy copies and records
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Courtesy copies and records: No paper courtesy copies of anything, including sealed documents. Administrative records are provided electronically only, with no physical copy filed; contact the courtroom deputy for filing instructions. For audio or video exhibits, email the courtroom deputy (Natalie Wood, natalie_wood@wawd.uscourts.gov).

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Scheduling, settlement, and contact
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Scheduling, settlement, and contact: Usually no Rule 16(b) conference; the court issues a scheduling order from the joint status report. Evaluate settlement at the outset and tell the court early if magistrate-judge mediation might help. On settlement, promptly file a notice stating how long dismissal papers will take. Chambers are in Washington, D.C.: call (202) 354-3330 or email Rothstein_Chambers@dcd.uscourts.gov, with all parties on the line or copied. Seattle courtroom: Suite 16106.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Discovery disputes: Try to resolve disputes first. For disputes that aren’t time-sensitive, use the LCR 37(a)(2) joint motion process; a unilateral, noted discovery motion is a last resort. Time-sensitive disputes: jointly email or call the courtroom deputy (Mary_Trent@wawd.uscourts.gov, (253) 882-3824) for an expedited conference, usually by phone or Zoom, with all concerned parties (LCR 7(i)). Submit a short joint statement of the dispute and each side’s position at least 24 hours ahead; it will typically be docketed. Complex legal questions may get a briefing schedule. Urgent disputes, such as mid-deposition: call the courtroom deputy to see if the judge is available, or ask for a law clerk, who can’t rule but may clarify. If unresolved, finish the deposition and raise the issue later.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Stipulated motions and protective orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Stipulated motions and protective orders (trap): File as a “stipulated motion,” not a “stipulation,” “agreed motion,” or “unopposed motion.” It may be noted for the day filed but won’t necessarily be signed that day. Include a proposed order and email a Word version to settleorders@wawd.uscourts.gov. Stipulated protective orders: the district’s model order is encouraged; under LCR 26(c)(2) also provide a redline showing departures from the model, which may be emailed to settleorders@wawd.uscourts.gov.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Oral argument and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Oral argument and courtesy copies: Most motions are decided without argument. The court decides whether to grant a request only after briefing is complete and will contact the parties to schedule. Courtesy copies are not required unless requested in a particular case.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Trial days and hours (trap)
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Trial days and hours (trap): Trial runs Tuesday through Friday. The courtroom opens about 8:15 a.m.; final pretrial matters at 8:30 or 8:45; the jury panel is sworn for voir dire at 9:00. Breaks about 10:30 and 3:00 (15 minutes each); lunch 12:00 to 1:30, with matters outside the jury’s presence at 1:15; recess at 4:30 p.m. Everyone must leave the courthouse by 5:00 p.m. unless court is in session; ask the courtroom deputy about leaving materials overnight.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. The jury may review admitted exhibits in paper and electronic form. Pre-mark every exhibit with cause number, party and exhibit number, and a blank “Admitted” line. Email a joint exhibit list in Word (auto-numbering off) to the courtroom deputy before trial. docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Jury instructions: The jury is instructed twice: before openings and after the evidence. The judge’s generic preliminary set (typically Ninth Circuit Model Instructions 1.1 through 1.11 criminal; 1.1A through 1.19 civil) is handed out at the pretrial conference, need not be submitted, and objections to it are raised there. Submit agreed instructions plus each side’s disputed ones with explanations and citations (LCR 51(e), (f)) and a proposed verdict form; the latest Ninth Circuit models are preferred. File on ECF and email Word to settleorders@wawd.uscourts.gov. Final instructions are settled with counsel at the end, with an opportunity to take exceptions, and each juror gets a copy.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Voir dire and deposition designations
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Voir dire and deposition designations: The court usually gives each side 15 minutes of voir dire, and a jury is usually sworn before the noon recess. The judge has jurors introduce themselves using topics on the board, reads a joint statement of the case (the parties supply it), and asks 15 standard questions (prior knowledge, acquaintance with parties, lawyers, or witnesses, legal, insurance, or accounting employment, prior lawsuits and jury service, military service, ability to follow the law, hardship). Besides LCR 32(e) highlighting, provide a separate chart for each deposition listing page and line of the testimony and objection, with columns for the ruling (grant/deny) and reason.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Courtroom technology
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Courtroom technology: If using courtroom equipment, get trained before the first day of trial, and bring your own equipment (laptops, videos, etc.) to the training to check compatibility. Questions: courtroom deputy Mary Trent, (253) 882-3824.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Contact
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Contact: Tacoma, Room 3100. Chambers: (253) 882-3850; courtroom deputy: (253) 882-3824. Proposed orders: settleorders@wawd.uscourts.gov.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Noting dates (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Noting dates (trap): Put the noting date in the caption and note on a weekday that is not a legal holiday. Same-day motions: stipulated, joint, or agreed motions; over-length requests; reconsideration; joint submissions; mediator appointment; default and default judgment; ex parte; recusal; and TROs. Per the posted sheet: motions for relief from a deadline and for protective orders are noted 14 days out (opposition 9 days, reply 14 days after filing); most other motions 21 days out (opposition 15, reply 21); dispositive motions, preliminary injunctions, Daubert motions, class certification, and forum changes (remand, transfer, arbitration) 28 days out (opposition 21, reply 28). The sheet is undated; check it against the current LCR 7(d). Motions in limine: note no later than 12 days before the pretrial conference. After briefing, the court decides whe

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Discovery disputes: Confer in good faith in person or by phone before seeking relief; consider the expedited joint procedure in LCR 37. Privilege logs must give enough detail to evaluate the claim; for attorney-client privilege, identify the attorney. If immediate involvement is needed, request a telephonic hearing under LCR 7(i); all counsel to the dispute must join the call to chambers at (206) 370-8930.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Default judgment (trap): Support the motion with a declaration and separately state principal, liquidated damages, pre- and post-judgment interest, and attorney’s fees, explaining how each was calculated. Provide evidence of the principal amount (attach the relevant contract portions if contract-based) and of entitlement to liquidated damages. State the interest rate and why, and for prejudgment interest the accrual date and its basis. Fee requests need a basis and a declaration from plaintiff’s counsel on the reasonable amount.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Motion form and length
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Motion form and length: The court may return over-length filings or decline to consider arguments beyond the LCR 7(e) limits. The sheet restates LCR 10 format (double spacing, 12-point text, 10-point footnotes, three inches at the top of page one).

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Sealing: Every motion to seal, including stipulated ones, must describe the documents specifically, give facts justifying sealing, and include a proposed order. Without agreement, file a properly noted motion before or with the document. Give at least 7 days’ notice before filing a document another party claims is confidential so a sealing motion can be filed with it. Tell the court what to do if sealing is denied (e.g., remove rather than unseal). Trial evidence, including confidential material, is generally public.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Mediation and settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Mediation and settlement conferences: In consent cases the judge enters an order stating whether the case is designated for LCR 39.1 mediation; the sample order sets a date to negotiate, has the parties pick and file a mediator (plaintiff applies if they can’t agree), and requires a mediator’s report. A settlement judge generally isn’t appointed until the parties have mediated. The courtroom deputy schedules the conference (Courtroom 12A, Seattle), and the court sets aside the entire day. Each trial attorney attends in person with a client or representative with full authority; failure to bring the right people or participate in good faith may draw costs and fees. Deliver a confidential memo (facts, issues, law, settlement proposal, efforts to date; helpful exhibits allowed) to chambers by 12:00 noon on the set date; don’t file or serve it.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Trial exhibits (trap): Deliver the original and one copy of exhibits to chambers no later than the pretrial conference date, in three-ring binders with numbered tabs, each exhibit clearly marked. Plaintiff numbers from 1; defendant continues with the next unused number. Don’t list duplicates; once listed in the pretrial order any party may use an exhibit. File exhibit and witness lists and revisions. Misdemeanor trials: unless otherwise directed, give the judge exhibits in tabbed three-ring binders on the trial date. The United States numbers from 1; defendants number from 1A.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Jury selection: Civil: tell the court before trial whether the case needs an extra-large pool or individual questioning of each prospective juror, and submit proposed voir dire questions in every case. Criminal: submit proposed voir dire questions five days before trial; only Class A misdemeanor defendants get a jury in misdemeanor cases. Jurors get random numbers, and the lowest-numbered sit in the box. The court describes the case, reads witness lists, has counsel make introductions, and screens for hardship and familiarity; counsel may usually question jurors within time limits the court sets. Challenges for cause are generally heard outside the jury’s presence. Each side normally gets three peremptories, noted alternately on a court form passed back and forth (plaintiff or the United States first); excused jurors are replaced from the benches in n

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Withdrawal and criminal motions
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Withdrawal and criminal motions: Withdrawal requires leave (GR 2(g)) except for changes within the same firm: file a written motion and supporting affidavit, which may be filed under seal if it contains privileged or prejudicial information. Motions to extend time to indict or file an information must state specific facts meeting the Speedy Trial Act; boilerplate (party agreement, a speedy trial waiver, time to negotiate) is insufficient alone. A defendant seeking the extension normally files a signed waiver. The sample civil consent form is marked “Do Not Electronically File.”

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Contact
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Contact: Seattle (Suite 12143). Proposed orders: tsuchidaorders@wawd.uscourts.gov. Chambers (206) 370-8930; courtroom deputy (206) 370-8421.

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Discovery disputes (trap): The court strictly construes meet-and-confer and strongly encourages resolving disputes without court involvement. For a telephonic motion under LCR 7(i), the moving party must make reasonable efforts to have all parties join; arrange it with deputy clerk Kelly Miller (kelly_miller@wawd.uscourts.gov, 253-882-3828).

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — Sealing

docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Conduct at trial (trap): Stand when court opens or recesses, when the jury enters or exits, and when addressing or addressed by the court; examine from the lectern; ask permission to approach the bench. Address remarks to the court and use surnames. One attorney per side per witness; the lawyer objecting on direct cross-examines. State only the legal ground for an objection. Sidebars are presumptively not tolerated except in extraordinary, unforeseen circumstances; make stipulation offers privately.

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Trial exhibits: Exhibits are handled electronically: admitted exhibits go to the jury through JEEPS, and DEPS is used for presentation. Display an offered exhibit to opposing counsel electronically first; hand any needed hard copy to the courtroom deputy. Before each session, show opposing counsel the exhibits you will offer; unobjected ones are admitted when offered, and objections are raised for ruling before the session opens. Counsel retrieve their own exhibits after trial.

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — New lawyers and courtroom rules
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. New lawyers and courtroom rules: The court encourages hearings conducted by lawyers practicing less than seven years, especially those who drafted the briefing; an experienced attorney may supplement their argument or questioning. Leave for supervised Rule 9 interns is freely granted, and multiple attorneys may argue for one party. Turn off mobile devices before entering. Give advance notice to use courtroom video displays. Pronouns and honorifics may be given in signature lines or to the in-court deputy.

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — Settlement conferences (trap)
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Settlement conferences (trap): On referral, the court promptly issues an order setting the date and procedures. Conferences are in person or, on the parties’ joint request, by Zoom. The posted example order (a 2018 template from Magistrate Judge Fricke) shows the likely terms. Under the example order, persons with ultimate settlement authority must be present or readily available by phone, and any party within 100 miles of the courthouse attends in person unless excused on a written request at least one week before. Plaintiff makes a demand at least 10 days before, and defendant responds at least one week before, even if the conference is set on shorter notice. Each side emails chambers a confidential memorandum of no more than 10 double-spaced pages, without exhibits absent extraordinary circumstances, not filed or served, covering liability disputes,

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Jury selection: The court voir dires a panel equal to the jurors to be seated (8 in most civil cases) plus all peremptory challenges; civil cases have no alternates. Sensitive issues and excuse requests are followed up with individual jurors separately via Zoom, and each panelist excused for cause is replaced before peremptories. Peremptory challenges are exercised simultaneously by written lists; overlapping strikes do not earn extra challenges, and jurors are seated from the lowest-numbered unchallenged panelist.

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — ESI and Individualized Trial Program
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. ESI and Individualized Trial Program: The page posts the district’s Model Agreement Regarding Discovery of ESI (e.g., disclosure of the five most likely custodians within 30 days; the requesting party may add up to 10 search terms within 14 days of the producer’s disclosure). The judge encourages the LCR 39.2 Individualized Trial Program; on agreement the court sets a case management conference, and trial is held within six months of approval.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Filings and contact
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Filings and contact: No courtesy copies unless the court orders otherwise. All PDFs must be text-searchable; PDFs longer than 14 pages need electronic bookmarks, and submissions longer than 14 pages (regardless of word count) need a table of contents. Use slip sheets (“Exhibit A” and nothing more) to separate exhibits. Avoid substantive footnotes; in-line citations preferred. Footnotes must be single spaced and 12-point or larger. Email the courtroom deputy (grant_cogswell@wawd.uscourts.gov) or whiteheadchambers@wawd.uscourts.gov, copying all counsel. No phone calls except emergencies ((206) 370-8700); no faxes. docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Extensions and scheduling (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Extensions and scheduling (trap): Parties may agree to extend the time to answer without filing anything. Initial scheduling order deadlines may be extended by contacting the courtroom deputy, with no stipulation filed. Deadlines falling before the dispositive motions deadline may be extended by a Stipulated Notice (not a motion) in the judge’s prescribed language, only if all parties stipulate (non-opposition won’t do), the deadline was not previously extended, and no hearing or related final-submission date changes. Otherwise dates are firm absent good cause, and the judge generally won’t shorten the gap between the dispositive motion deadline and trial. Don’t file notices of unavailability; they have no effect on deadlines.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Motions (trap): Meet and confer before any Rule 12(b) motion to see if amendment can avoid it; the motion must include a certification of conferral. Don’t oppose a timely motion, or withhold a stipulation, to amend. Daubert motions are due by the dispositive motion deadline and can’t be raised or renewed as motions in limine. Oral argument may be requested but is not granted as a matter of course; the deputy schedules it, and the noting date is not the hearing date. Less experienced attorneys and those from historically underrepresented backgrounds are encouraged to argue, and more than one attorney may argue per party.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Cross-motions for summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Cross-motions for summary judgment (trap): Anticipated cross-motions must be briefed in four sequential briefs, not six: opening 8,400 words; combined opening/opposition 10,500; combined opposition/reply 10,500; reply 4,200. The court assumes the defendant files first, but the parties may choose. File a stipulated motion proposing the schedule and word limits before the first brief; all briefing must be complete by the dispositive motion deadline.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Discovery (trap): Discovery motions are a last resort. Good-faith conferral requires affirmative suggestions and compromise, not just stating positions; the court will deny or strike a motion for failure to confer. Motions must state the grounds and relief with specificity or be denied. The court urges use of the LCR 37(a)(2) expedited joint motion procedure. Don’t file initial disclosures or expert reports unless ordered or at issue. Deposition objections must be concise and non-suggestive (e.g., “Objection, compound”); no conferring with the witness while a question is pending except on privilege; instruct not to answer only to preserve privilege, enforce a court limit, or present a Rule 30(d)(3) motion.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Hearings
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Hearings: Hearings are in person in Courtroom 16A, Seattle, unless ordered otherwise. On Zoom (if warranted): each participant needs their own camera and microphone, video on, muted unless speaking, no screenshare, professional attire, a quiet room (not a car); recording is illegal. Telephonic proceedings use the court’s conference line with credentials from the deputy; use a landline if possible and identify yourself each time you speak.

docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Criminal cases: All motions, including motions to continue trial and motions in limine, are due no later than 28 days before trial; motions in limine raised later in a trial brief will be stricken. In multi-defendant cases, consult codefendants about joint or stipulated motions. A motion to continue trial needs a speedy trial waiver running at least 30 days past the proposed new date, and the deputy must first confirm the date fits the calendar. Stipulated or unopposed continuance motions may be noted same-day. Juries of 12 with one or two alternates chosen randomly before deliberations; government 6 and defendants jointly 10 peremptories, alternating from the government. Exhibits: one physical and one electronic set to the deputy 5 days before trial; government from 1, defense from A-1. Follow CrR 30 for instructions.

docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Courtroom etiquette: Argue and question from the lectern; don’t approach the jury or a witness without permission. Stand when speaking if able. Phones must be off in session; disable laptop voice assistants. Share honorifics or pronouns with the deputy or when appearing; ask the deputy about accommodations.

docs.t: Judge James L. Robart (W.D. Wash.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge James L. Robart, W.D. Wash.. Default judgment (trap): Insufficient motions are denied. Support the motion with a declaration under LCR 55; state separately the principal, liquidated damages, pre- and post-judgment interest, and attorney’s fees, with a concise explanation of each calculation. Amounts whose calculation is unclear won’t be awarded. Prove the principal (attach relevant contract portions and any data needed, such as hours worked) and any entitlement to liquidated damages. Justify any non-§ 1961 interest rate, include all interest calculations, and state the prejudgment-interest start date and why. Fees need a stated basis and a counsel declaration on the reasonable amount.

docs.x: Judge James L. Robart, W.D. Wash.. Peremptories go on a form passed back and forth, plaintiff first, so neither side wastes a challenge; avoid challenging jurors numbered too high to be reached. Jurors are the lowest-numbered panelists remaining. Civil: six to twelve jurors, no alternates, and ordinarily three peremptories per side. Criminal: twelve jurors plus one or two alternates (the court asks whether the parties want to select the alternates), with normally six peremptories

docs.x: Judge Richard A. Jones, W.D. Wash.. Discovery, sealing, and default judgment: Use the LCR 37 expedited joint procedure where motions are needed. Attach the relevant contract portions; amounts whose calculation is unclear won’t be awarded.

docs.x: Judge Robert J. Bryan, W.D. Wash.. Courtroom protocol (trap): Address the judge as “your Honor” or “the Court,” not “Judge”; refer to witnesses, counsel, and parties by surname unless leave is given. Speak from beside counsel table or the lectern, and rise to object or address the court. Don’t approach opposing counsel, the bench, a witness, the reporter, or the clerk without leave; hand papers for the court or a witness to the clerk or bailiff. Be punctual, have enough witnesses for each day, and arrange chalkboards, tripods, or other visual aids with the clerk in advance so they can be set up while court is not in session. No gestures, expressions, or comments showing approval or disapproval.

docs.t: Judge Robert J. Bryan (W.D. Wash.) — Examination and objections (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert J. Bryan, W.D. Wash.. Examination and objections (trap): Only one attorney per party may examine a witness, and only the attorney conducting (or to conduct) that witness’s examination may object. State only the legal basis of an objection (e.g., “leading,” “hearsay”) without elaboration or argument unless asked. No questions restating or paraphrasing prior testimony, and no extraneous remarks during examination. Don’t make motions (e.g., for mistrial) or offer stipulations in the jury’s hearing; raise them at the first recess or sidebar. Don’t put before the jury matter you expect to draw a sustained objection; take it up outside the jury’s presence.

docs.t: Judge Robert J. Bryan (W.D. Wash.) — Voir dire (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert J. Bryan, W.D. Wash.. Voir dire (trap): The judge explains the case and burden of proof, gives preliminary instructions, and conducts general voir dire, including questions submitted by counsel. Counsel may then question the panel as a group and individual jurors. Not allowed: repeated questions, questions anticipating instructions not yet given, asking jurors to predict a verdict on assumed facts, soliciting opinions on laws or legal terms, irrelevant or rapport-building questions, argument, unfair or embarrassing questions, and questions jurors can’t possibly answer. The judge will interrupt without waiting for an objection.

Propose a trial date and work backward: Daubert motions heard by the dispositive-motion deadline, at least 12 weeks from that deadline to the final pretrial conference, and at least 2 weeks from the conference to trial. The judge expects many cases to be tried within 12 months of the case management conference. Scheduled dates move only by court order on a joint statement of no more than 3 pages showing particularized good cause; trial dates, usually set at the initial conference, move only for compelling good cause. docs.t: Judge Haywood Gilliam (N.D. Cal.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Haywood Gilliam, N.D. Cal.. Discovery: Raise disputes early by a joint letter of no more than 5 pages. The court may refer all discovery to a magistrate judge, whose procedures then govern. Leave enough time to resolve disputes before the discovery cutoff; pending disputes will not extend deadlines absent truly compelling reasons.

docs.t: Judge Haywood Gilliam (N.D. Cal.) — Sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Haywood Gilliam, N.D. Cal.. Sealing (trap): Each sealing motion must say whether the compelling-reasons or good-cause standard applies and why, with a specific, narrowly tailored showing for each document. Generic “competitive harm” claims almost always fail. The L.R. 79-5(c)(3) proposed-order table must list, per item, the public and sealed docket numbers, document name, portions to seal, and reasons with citations. A designating party’s L.R. 79-5(f)(3) declaration needs a new proposed order in that format, and revised redacted and unredacted versions if it seeks less sealing.

docs.t: Judge Haywood Gilliam (N.D. Cal.) — Civil trial
docs.x: Judge Haywood Gilliam, N.D. Cal.. Civil trial: Trial runs Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m.; counsel arrive by 8 a.m. A flash drive of exhibits goes to the Clerk’s Office 7 days before trial; file form exhibit and witness lists 3 days before. Pre-mark exhibits with trial exhibit stickers in agreed number blocks, defendant’s after plaintiff’s; defendant withdraws duplicates without renumbering. Stipulate to admissibility, or at least authenticity and foundation, 14 days before the conference. Disclose witnesses and their exhibits by noon the day before they testify; an unready witness usually means resting. Confer each evening in person or by phone (not email) on next-day exhibits and demonstratives, and file any 5-page dispute statements by midnight. Daily transcript requests (CAND 435) are due 14 days before trial; extra equipment needs a request and proposed order 7 days before.

docs.t: Judge Haywood Gilliam (N.D. Cal.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Haywood Gilliam, N.D. Cal.. Criminal matters: For a plea agreement, the government emails it to HSGcrd@cand.uscourts.gov (all counsel copied) by 2 p.m. the Friday before the plea; for an open plea, defense notifies the court by then. Before plea and sentencing of out-of-custody defendants, the government emails whether 18 U.S.C. § 3143 mandatory remand applies by the Monday before. Joint pretrial statement, trial memoranda, witness and exhibit lists, joint jury instructions, voir dire, and verdict forms are due 7 days before the pretrial conference (Word copies of instructions, voir dire, and verdict forms to HSGpo). Motions in limine 14 days before, oppositions 7 days before, 5 pages each, no replies. docs.t: Judge Haywood Gilliam (N.D. Cal.) — Patent cases
docs.x: Judge Haywood Gilliam, N.D. Cal.. Patent cases: Patent disclosure disputes and motions to amend or strike contentions typically go to the magistrate judge. The P.L.R. 4-3 joint claim construction statement must be truly joint, side by side per the model chart, with the patents attached. The court generally construes no more than 10 terms; leave for more must be sought by L.R. 7-11 motion at least 2 weeks before the joint statement is due, or only the first 10 listed will be construed and sanctions may follow. Tutorial: 45 minutes per side, no argument, preferably by someone other than counsel. Claim construction hearing: 90 minutes per side, run as oral argument, not a PowerPoint lecture. Testimony requires an L.R. 7-11 motion at least 7 days ahead.

docs.t: Judge Beth Labson Freeman (N.D. Cal.) — Chambers copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Beth Labson Freeman, N.D. Cal.. Chambers copies (trap): Paper copies are required only for pleadings and briefing and evidence on substantive motions, delivered to the Clerk’s Office by noon the next court day (the order says within one business day). Never send chambers copies of administrative or other non-substantive motions, including sealing motions. Copies must be printed from ECF with the header, single-sided, 2-hole punched at the top, and stapled or prong-fastened, with numbered bottom tabs (not side tabs) between exhibits. Exhibits over six inches thick go in binders; final pretrial conference copies are 3-hole punched on the left. docs.t: Judge Beth Labson Freeman (N.D. Cal.) — Page limits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Beth Labson Freeman, N.D. Cal.. Page limits (trap): 25/25/15 pages for motions under Rules 12, 23, 56, 59, or 65, judgment on the pleadings, FLSA collective certification, anti-SLAPP, social security appeals, and claim construction. All other motions without a set limit (for example remand, arbitration, leave to amend, stay, default judgment, sanctions, fees, interlocutory appeal) are 10/10/5. Limits are per side, not per party, and a party’s own motion plus a joined motion count together. The notice of motion counts toward the limit. Each side gets 25 pages total for all post-answer dispositive motions combined (oppositions 25, replies 15), and one summary judgment motion per party. Daubert motions: 10 pages per expert, 25 pages total per side. All post-trial motions: one brief of 25 pages per side.

docs.t: Judge Beth Labson Freeman (N.D. Cal.) — Briefing and formatting (trap)
docs.x: Judge Beth Labson Freeman, N.D. Cal.. Briefing and formatting (trap): Any stipulated briefing schedule must leave at least 14 days (preferably 21) between the final brief and the hearing. All text, including footnotes and quotations, must be at least 12-point and double-spaced. No citations to authority or evidence in footnotes; generally no more than 5 footnotes per brief, and excessive ones are disregarded. No incorporation by reference of arguments from other briefs (except among parties sharing page limits). Highlight cited portions of depositions and long documents in yellow only. Evidentiary objections go in the brief. Argument supporting a request for judicial notice counts against the page limit. Proposed orders go in Word to BLFpo@cand.uscourts.gov the day they are e-filed. Do not communicate ex parte with the judge or chambers.

docs.t: Judge Beth Labson Freeman (N.D. Cal.) — Summary judgment and Daubert timing
docs.x: Judge Beth Labson Freeman, N.D. Cal.. Summary judgment and Daubert timing: Summary judgment motions must be heard at least 90 days before trial; the court generally reserves a compliant date at the initial CMC. Daubert motions must be heard at least 60 days before trial, or may instead be brought as motions in limine (one expert per motion).

docs.t: Judge Beth Labson Freeman (N.D. Cal.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Beth Labson Freeman, N.D. Cal.. Sealing: Each sealing motion under Civil L.R. 79-5(c) and each designating-party declaration under 79-5(f)(3) must include a four-column chart (ECF or exhibit number, document, portions to seal, reasons with declaration cites), one row per document, and be emailed in Word to BLFpo@cand.uscourts.gov the day of filing. If the court allows narrower sealing than the public versions reflect, the filing party must refile public versions within 7 days unless a renewed motion or declaration is filed.
